speechtext: I should like to address two questions to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. 1. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister, a copy of which I supplied to him just a few minutes ago after he came into the house. The C.B.C. reported this morning that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) had induced this government to provide financial help to Newfoundland to move people into more populous areas. If the report is true, will the government also be prepared to help other provinces with similar problems, for example with respect to displaced coal miners in the provinces of Alberta and Nova Scotia?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF WORKERS TO MORE POPULOUS AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that this is one of the usual arrangements made by the
(Mr. Castleden.]

Department of Labour to provide alternative employment in areas where labour is required from areas where it is not required, and that the Minister of Labour can further develop the answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF WORKERS TO MORE POPULOUS AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) brought to my attention the plight of families living in the small community of St. Brendan's, Newfoundland. From representations made it appeared that the prospects of their being able to maintain a livelihood in that community were extremely slim indeed. Consequently it seemed to me that it was worth the effort of having representatives of the Department of Labour and the national employment service jointly look into the situation. They were asked to do so and they have been doing so for some little time now.
That procedure is in general accord with activities that have taken place through the two agencies in other places in Canada during recent years. Sometimes the stress has been in the Department of Labour and assistance has been given in vocational training as in Westville, Nova Scotia and in my own constituency in Marysville, New Brunswick. Sometimes it has been the national employment service in co-operation with such a committee as Mr. Manning created in Alberta for moving families out from small coal mining towns to where they could get jobs elsewhere. In that case the provincial governments did not ask for financial assistance in moving but they did ask for and receive close co-operation and help in other phases of the move by our employees of the national employment service.
In this particular case I must say that I have not had the official report yet from my officials in Newfoundland but if it is as was outlined in this morning's broadcast, I will recommend favourable consideration on the matter.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF WORKERS TO MORE POPULOUS AREAS
speechtext: As a supplementary question, may I ask whether any legislation will be required in order to enable the government to implement this plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF WORKERS TO MORE POPULOUS AREAS
speechtext:
No. There has been authority now for four years giving the Minister of Labour authority to investigate and survey what we have been accustomed to call in the past special "depressed areas" and, if the situation warranted it, to work out a plan with the provincial authorities and to recommend it to cabinet for the purpose of bringing relief to bear with respect to moving workers from that area.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver East, Mr. Speaker, asked if I had received a letter from Mr. George F. Edwards, president of the senior citizens' association of British Columbia, under date of July 10. I find there is no record of any such letter having been received, but I have seen a mimeographed copy of the letter which was apparently sent to other people as well. The letter dealt with the policy of housing senior citizens.
The situation is as I set out when presenting my estimates earlier this year. Our general policy, of course, recognizes the position of our senior citizens. In government-sponsored public housing projects for low income groups, the government feels it is fitting and proper that a proportion of the units should be available to senior citizens in the appropriate income groups, but I think it would be unwise to assign any public housing projects exclusively to any particular class of Canadians. What we aim at is a good cross-section of all classes, races and creeds that comprise Canadian citizenship.
On the other hand, where private enterprise takes the initiative under the terms of the National Housing Act, even where the housing project is built largely with government funds as in the case of limited dividend operations, the owner may house anybody he wishes so long as the tenants conform to the income requirements.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES IMPORTS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Can the minister advise whether the government has completed its inquiry into the matter of importation into Canada of motor vehicles and parts from the United States? If so, what action is the government prepared to take in respect of this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES IMPORTS
speechtext:
The matter has been investigated. The postcards which were received 67509-4071
Inquiries of the Ministry in considerable numbers referred to the fact that in 1950 we imported from the United States 3,154 vehicles and last year 27,392 passenger cars valued at $58,886,000. The two situations are hardly comparable, in that in 1950 we were exercising import control' on a number of more or less luxury items which included automobiles, and therefore 1950 was an unusual year in that regard.
However, our imports of automobiles usually run as a proportion of the sales of automobiles in Canada, and the ratio runs between 5 per cent and 7 per cent. In 1951 we produced 282,714 units and imported 14,050 units, which was 5 per cent of the Canadian production. In 1952 we produced 283,534 units and imported 13,828 units or 5 per cent of Canadian production. In 1953 we produced 360,385 units and imported 23,501 units or 6| per cent of Canadian production. In 1954 we produced 287,191 units and imported 17,954 units, or 64 per cent of Canadian production. In 1955, we produced 374,945 units and imported 27,392 units, or 7| per cent of Canadian production.
It has been the policy of Canadian automobile manufacturers to produce models that sell in large volume in Canada and to import those models where the volume does not warrant the cost of tooling. This applies particularly to the higher priced cars, which have been in increasing demand in Canada in recent years as a direct result of the high level of prosperity in this country. Our importation of parts increases with our increased production of motor cars in Canada. In other words, the importation of parts increases proportionately with the production of motor cars in Canada.
It seems obvious from our study that there is nothing abnormal in the present situation. The impact of the strike at General Motors was felt during that period. More cars than usual were imported, but aside from that the situation seems to be quite normal.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES IMPORTS
speechtext: Do I understand that the minister's figures refer exclusively to the importation of United States cars and do not include the importation of other cars?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES IMPORTS
speechtext:
No, the imports from abroad are on a declining scale, as against the peak years. There are certainly fewer foreign cars imported, that is cars from overseas, than was the case three or four years ago, and fewer than immediately after the war. However, the question referred particularly to imports from the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore):
That Bill No. 442 be not now read a third time, but that it be read a third time this day six months.
I do not move this motion with any desire to kill the bill nor with any desire to make it impossible for the government to complete legislation of this kind. There are some things within the bill with which we thoroughly agree. We think, for example, that inclusion of the equalization principle in the bill is good and necessary, particularly at this stage when there are provinces in Canada that are struggling to overcome their financial difficulties and trying to establish themselves in an expansion movement that will eventually help them to help themselves. We think that the equalization principle is sound and we are prepared to go along with it. We believe also that the principle of stabilization of revenues is good, and that is something we commend; we are not against that at all. We also believe that the increased refunds of tax collections to the provinces, provided by this bill, is something better than the provinces have had under the tax rental agreement.
I want you to note, Mr. Speaker, that I refer to the payments to the provinces as increased refunds of tax collections from the provinces. I like to look upon them as such. It is not a question of this government giving the provinces anything that does not belong to them. We have already made clear that in our view what the government of Canada is doing under these agreements is refunding tax collections from the provinces in a certain measure back to the provinces to help them to get along and to make it unnecessary for the provinces to impose double taxation with all the confusion that is bound to result from that sort of thing.

However, as I pointed out last night very briefly when I moved the amendment, the wording of the title and the wording of the bill itself at various places seem to indicate that the government of Canada feels that it is allowing the provinces something. I wanted to establish very definitely the principle that there is a partnership in this country and that what the government is doing is making available under a tax-sharing plan something that already belongs to the provinces but that it is being granted them under an agreement with which the provinces are ready to go along.
We look upon this bill as imposing a unilateral decision by this government on the provinces. That is our chief criticism of it. We feel it is unwise yet to go ahead with the bill before the provinces have considered the wording and have been able to convey to the government their feelings with regard to the whole bill. We look upon it as a denial of the partnership principle which is necessary if we are going to have a smoothworking federal democracy. The present bill and the present attitude of the government deny that partnership principle. The government's attitude seems to convey to the provinces the idea, "We are prepared to do something for you, to allow you this or allow you that, but you have to take it on our terms." I think that in principle that is wrong in every way.
We think there is still time to rectify the mistake that has been made in not submitting the bill to the provinces for their approval before it is enacted into law. That is the reason why we move the six months' hoist. We think the six months will give the Minister of Finance time to submit the bill to the provincial governments in conference, and he would still have time to have the bill made law before the end of the present fiscal year, when the old tax transfer agreements terminate.
We feel that the government and all the house should give careful consideration to this six months' period during which something further can be done to help the provinces to feel they are partners in this great Canada. I want to say that there seems to be very little noise made these days in defence of provincial rights. We want to defend those provincial rights. We do not want them to sell their birthright for a mess of pottage, and that is exactly what they do when they are dragged along with a unilateral proposal of this kind. So we feel very definitely that the government should make another effort, and I think they would be successful in carrying the provinces along with them if they would call a conference and try to satisfy the provinces that they

I shall not argue the point as to equality, because after all there is not an equality between a province and this parliament. The British North America Act very clearly stipulated, or first of all stated, that there were three provinces which came into confederation. I think it is noteworthy that in the British North America Act those three provinces were made four provinces and it was stipulated that each province should have a legislature and that there should be one parliament for Canada. I have noticed with a good deal of misgiving that the legislatures of some of the provinces have been promoting themselves to parliaments of late and referring to the leading minister in those legislatures as the prime minister. To my mind that is completely wrong, and I think it is leading to a great deal of improper talk across Canada about the relation of the provinces and the dominion.
I could not support the six months' hoist which would kill the bill. I think the suggestion that there might be further conferences is a good suggestion, but let us be quite clear as to what the position is as between the provinces and this parliament. I readily admit that the provinces require more revenues, that


the municipalities require more revenues, but the dominion, with the consent of the provinces, has assumed more and more obligations that were probably originally intended to be assumed by the provinces themselves. That is particularly true with regard to property and civil rights in the social security and other measures that we have adopted and I hope will continue to expand in this parliament. It seems to me that while negotiation between the provinces and the dominion is right and proper we should be very careful indeed that we do not accept the view that this parliament has not a right to make decisions of this sort.
Since the tax agreements expire on the 31st of March next and since in my opinion it is quite essential that we shall have something ready and the provinces shall know that we have got something ready and make their proper preparations accordingly, the six months' hoist, which would bring this matter into next January or February because we are at the end of July, would mean that neither the dominion nor the provinces would have sufficient time to make their plans. Consequently, while we would have liked to have seen further negotiations after the second reading of the bill we cannot support-I am sure I speak for those with me although I have not had time to consult them-something that would kill the bill and make it impossible to do the thing that is essential for the welfare of the country by the first of April of next year.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on second reading of this bill on July 23 I sought to indicate the reasons why we of Her Majesty's loyal opposition feel that the bill does not do justice to the provinces nor to the municipalities of this country and why for those reasons we could not support the bill on second reading. At that time, sir, we urged a change of heart on the part of the dominion government and a recognition by it of the constitutional position of the provinces and the extremely onerous responsibilities that are cast today by the constitution upon the provincial and municipal governments of this country.
We said then that this whole question should be further reviewed and that there should be a new conference between the federal and provincial authorities if the federal government will show some change of heart and some adequate recognition of the constitutional position of the provinces and the needs and problems of the provincial and municipal governments. That is our position today. There ought to be a reopening of this whole question between the federal and provincial governments. No time should be lost in that regard, and out of that conference should come a very much better deal for the provinces and the municipalities.
It is true that the present measure does offer some improvement over the fiscal agreements that have been in effect during the past five years and which will expire on March 31 next, but the improvement is not nearly adequate and it does not afford sufficient reason for the provincial governments being tied up for the next five years, particularly at a period of tremendous national development of resources which throws such an abnormally heavy financial burden upon the provincial and municipal governments and which at the same time produces tremendous revenues for the federal treasury.
We have now reached almost the end of July. The present fiscal arrangements continue until March 31 next, eight months away. I think there is merit in the amendment that has been introduced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). It does not deal with the bill finally but in effect it says to this government that we think that, in the next six months, they ought to carry out the plain duty that lies before them of taking this matter back in conference to the provincial premiers as spokesmen of the provincial governments and the municipal governments of this country; and that they should take it
6420	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements back not in the arbitrary and rigid attitude which has characterized the approach of the federal government to this problem but rather with a view to arriving at a settlement and agreement in the spirit which the fathers of confederation exhibited when they met to overcome much greater difficulties than those which confront the federal and provincial governments today in approaching their common fiscal problems and relations.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I think the house ought to support the amendment which has been introduced. It affords an opportunity which, if it is used by the federal government as it ought to be used, could result-with a wholesome Canadian attitude on their part-in a very much more satisfactory disposition of the problem of common fields of taxation and very great fiscal responsibilities in a period of rapid development of the resources of this country. Within that six months' period we would hope that the government would come back to parliament with a very much better scheme than the one embodied in the present bill. As I sought to say in speaking on second reading two days ago, we would be happy to come back here to a fall session or to a session at any time in order to deal with a better measure, one that will afford adequate recognition of the constitutional position of the provinces and the heavy responsibilities Which they and the municipalities bear.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we consider that we are making a proposal that is good for all of Canada and that is good for the provinces whose administration of the resources that lie within their boundaries is going to have so much to do with the health of the whole Canadian economy in the years to come. If they are not to be healthy provincial administrations in a sound fiscal position, I submit to this house that the development of our resources is going to be checked. The administration of these resources, by our constitution, is confided to the provincial governments. They must be strong fiscally if they are to carry out their constitutional responsibilities. If they are hampered or if they are placed in a strait-jacket in that regard over a period of these next five years, which may be a period of critical importance in the development of this country, the federal government and the federal treasury are going to suffer.
We therefore say, Mr. Speaker, that here is an opportunity now to use valuable time- for no time should be lost-to re-examine the problem, to bring together the provincial premiers, and for the federal government to exhibit to them a wholesome recognition of the constitutional position of the provinces

and the responsibilities which, under that constitution, fall on the provincial and municipal governments. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, we propose to support the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Peace River.
Here are six precious months. Let this federal government use them to good advantage, to wholesome advantage, in the interests of the whole of Canada. If they do so, Mr. Speaker, I am sure this house will have the opportunity of giving approval to legislation that will represent a far more equitable distribution of the yield from common tax fields, a far more adequate recognition of the position that the provinces hold under our scheme of confederation; and that will not leave provinces and municipalities faced with colossal burdens and colossal expenditures far beyond their present capacity to meet, as is the situation today.

I rise only to speak to this amendment because, up to this point so far as I know, no voice has been raised from my province regarding this legislation. The conclusion might be erroneously drawn, therefore, that Prince Edward Island is satisfied with the agreement. We believe that there are two problems which this agreement tries to meet. One is a fair division of the tax resources of the country between the central government on the one hand and the provinces on the other. We feel that this legislation does not go far enough towards meeting the needs of the provinces. As a matter of fact, there seems to be reluctance on the part of the central government to admit that the provinces have any rights, or rights to the extent the provinces believe they have in any case. As a matter of fact some of the provinces believe the central government is trying to sell them a ride on their own horse.
When the colonies which now form Canada came together, the fathers of confederation believed a reasonable division of tax resources was made to meet the needs of the central government on the one hand and the provinces on the other. As I have already said, that is one of the purposes of this legislation, to bring that division up to date. There is another problem which this legislation should meet. It should try to remove the injustice which is the lot of some provinces as compared to others in that they have not been favoured to an equal extent by confederation.

We in the maritimes feel that we have contributed greatly to the success of confederation generally, and that we have not benefited in proportion over the years. The governments of the maritime provinces, and that of Prince Edward Island in particular, have striven to put forward their just claims in that regard and have met with varying success throughout the years.
On one occasion the then minister of finance said, and I quote from Sir Thomas White very briefly when he was minister of finance in 1912-I do not intend to take up much time of the house:
I have become enthusiastic about it, and I say that Prince Edward Island from the date of union has been hardly treated, and I believe that her dwindling population is, to a very large extent, due to the fact that she has been deprived of the subsidies to which she was justly and reasonably entitled from the dominion since confederation. I hope to show to the satisfaction of the house that this grant is not only justified, but abundantly justified. I hope that a new era will dawn for the province of Prince Edward Island when it gets this enlarged subsidy.
Then, the leader of the opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, had this to say:
The one reason only which has impressed me- and it is not a constitutional reason, it is not a legal reason, it is simply a reason of equity-is the fact that Prince Edward Island has not profited by confederation.
As a result of these points of view the maritimes, and Prince Edward Island perhaps in particular, had these claims satisfied to some degree. Please give me a chance to say so before you object. That is common sense, is it not?
As far as I can judge, it is quite possible for the minister to call a provincial conference as soon as this session is closed and, with the provinces, devise a bill which will be satisfactory to the provinces and then draft that bill and bring it into the House of Commons in the early days of the next session and have that bill passed before the time on which the other agreements expire. I think it is not beyond the possibility of this house to do that. I am sure hon. members would be quite ready to expedite the passage of such a bill.
The greatest anxiety that we feel as a group is that a precedent might be set, as I pointed out the other day, under which there will be a tendency to weaken provincial autonomy and consequently undermine the sanctity of the British North America Act. That was our whole reason in introducing the amendment last night. If the change had been made in the title of the bill which was envisaged by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in his amendment, then there would have been written into the bill a specific guarantee of the sanctity of the British North America Act and we would have had no further objection whatsoever.
It has to be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that while we are dealing with provinces which are not populous at the present time, which number their populations in, say, 1J million, provinces such as Alberta and British Columbia, we are dealing with infants just beginning to grow into giants. Those provinces in 50 years time may have

Now, measures we take in this house could easily abrogate the constitutional guarantees Of freedom of action which those provinces in those days with their great populations would need in the most urgent way. Therefore, in every move we make today we are building for the future.
I know there is a great deal of pressure at the present time to centralize control everywhere, as I pointed out when I spoke on a previous occasion. But that pressure to centralize is Marxism; it is communist, pure and simple, and it is being made by the agents of communism, the originators of communism, whom I characterized the other day as Turko-Mongolian reds descendants of Esau.
There will be those who say, "I do not understand". Well, there was a time when I could not understand, but I understand now. They are not the kind of people our forefathers were. Our forefathers, as early as we can find a record of them at all, insisted on local self-government and they met in their villages and elsewhere and decided what they would do and in large measure they governed themselves in their villages. Going back to constitutional history in Great Britain, you will And that everywhere written.
Our concept is just exactly diametrically opposite to the Marxist concept. Marxists are working for the centralization of power in the world so their people who now constitute only a very few millions of the world's total population shall be able to dictate absolutely the conditions of life for all the billions of people in the world. That is the object of centralization.
I indicated the other day that Major C. H. Douglas said that the British North America Act and the constitution of Australia are the two most perfect constitutions in the world. Perfect for what? Marxism? No. Communism? No. Turko-Mongolian reds? Oh no, it is just poison to all of them; but for British people, Anglo-Saxon-Celts, it is a perfect constitution and we want to keep it so. It is our anxiety in this group, lest something be done here in this bill by this house which might endanger those of the future, that has led us to take the position we have taken and to move this amendment.
I hope it is perfectly clear there is no desire to kill the bill or to kill the principle.

All right just a minute. I shall be glad to have your questions but let us have them in order, please, so the question


will appear on Hansard just as it was asked, and my answer will be recorded in exactly the way it was spoken. That is the only way in which the record will be worth while. If anyone wants to ask a question let him indicate his desire and I will answer it. The matter we are discussing today is too important to appear as a garbled report such as the Hansard people, capable and efficient as they are, can only produce if they cannot hear the questions that are asked and the answers which I give.
Now let me proceed to point out once more that we are not opposed to the principle of sharing taxation at all but we are opposed to the principle of weakening in any way the British North America Act.
When I was speaking the other day I pointed out that beyond a shadow of a doubt in my opinion the establishment of the Bank of Canada was accomplished by these very people who were seeking to centralize power and to put in Canada an agency through which they could control the destiny of Canada from London, for example, or from Basel, Switzerland, a thing which is not necessary at all.
We can control our own money here in this country and we want to keep that control right where it is.
I have said that we approve of the idea of sharing taxation.
I want to speak directly to Ontario for a few minutes, if I might. We have nothing but sympathy for the people of Ontario and for the province of Ontario and its needs for revenue. We fully realize that as industrial development has taken place in Ontario the burdens of government have increased, and inevitably so, if for no other reason than because the water supply which is used by industry has to be guaranteed by the provinces and the water has to be cleansed after industry is finished with it. All of these things constitute a burden on Ontario, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) pointed out when he was speaking, and there are many other ways in which he indicated that the burdens of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, our great industrial provinces, are greatly enhanced by the development of industry.
In case a depression comes along, what will be the position of the provinces in which there is a great labour population to become unemployed? It is immediately obvious that those industrial provinces, if they have wise governments, are going to be taking precautions to provide for situations of that sort. Because of all these things, I speak with great sympathy for the people of Ontario and Quebec, the highly industrialized provinces

of this nation. I am thankful they are where they are. I rejoice in them; they are a blessing to Canada.
One of the main things we have in mind in Alberta however, is that we realize in the case of a big company manufacturing agricultural implements or automobiles for instance, much of the profit of the company is made out in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba. We ask, is there any reason why that portion of the money which is made in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba should not be drawn off by a wise taxation policy in Ottawa and returned to us in those provinces where the money was made? We see no reason why that should not be done. Beyond that, there certainly must be great caution not to draw away from Ontario or Quebec the means of supporting the conditions which must obtain in those provinces.
I wish now to say a word or two about the four maritime provinces. One reason we do not trust this government in the main, and the whole set-up today, is simply that they are making no provisions whatsoever for permanently establishing the four maritime provinces in such a way that they can get along by themselves.
It is not good for a province to be on relief. The people in the maritime provinces do not want to be on relief. The people there are as fine as any people in the Dominion of Canada and probably there are no finer people in the British commonwealth. They are capable, independent, proud and self-sustaining. It is a source of the utmost mortification to them to have to come to Ottawa for more and more handouts, more and more subsidies and subventions and all that sort of thing. It is repulsive to them. The people in the maritime provinces ought to be put in a position where that kind of thing is not necessary. Up to the present time there has not been one single move made on the part of any Liberal administration since 1935 to enable those provinces to support themselves.
I appreciate all that was said by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) the other day. I rejoice that assistance has been sent down to those provinces, but let us see what it was that happened to those provinces when they came into confederation-New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and later Prince Edward Island.
In the first place they lost control of their financial affairs. Very, very soon the ownership of the banks in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia passed into the hands of companies whose head offices were located in Toronto or Montreal. This meant that the policy of those banks in those provinces was
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements no longer subject to the control of the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. That was one of the most serious things that occurred to them, just as it was with us out in Alberta. In Alberta in 1935, when the Social Credit government took over, do you know what we were paying for loans from banks? Eight per cent. The member for Peace River points out that even though the statutory rate was 7 per cent, those banks were charging 8 per cent. That 8 per cent was increasing the difficulty of the producers of every single commodity in the province of Alberta. It was a burden imposed upon us which we had no way under the sun of alleviating or removing.
Our railroad freight rates were imposed upon us. There is not a thing we can do about it except complain, and I should not be surprised if the day comes when we will tell the two central governments, "Keep your railways at home; we shall build our own, because we are simply not going to be saddled with the increasing freight rates which render it impossible for us to live." Once you get the people determined, they will get somewhere. We were, I repeat, under a set of freight rates which bled us white, both when the freight was coming out to us and when it was going back from us.
The same kind of condition exists in the maritimes, and there is nothing they can do about it. If they fail in a business way, we blame them, when as a matter of fact we ought to blame the policy of the government which allows the railways to prey on them as they do.
The maritimes moreover lost the power to determine what goods they were going to admit. Raw materials which they had been accustomed to getting from the United States and elsewhere they were prevented from bringing in, because the central government imposed a tariff against those goods. No matter how much those provinces needed those goods, they had to pay that tariff. The result was that many industries in the maritimes, I understand, were put in the position where they simply had to die. We cannot enable the maritimes to run their own affairs until we overcome that difficulty.
Furthermore, there were customary markets for which they had arranged with various other countries. Those markets were closed in large measure because of tariff policies and fiscal policies here in Ottawa.
What can we do to make up to the maritime provinces for these disadvantages that have been imposed upon them by being in the Canadian union? People will say, "I do not know what to do." "I do not know what to do" is just not good enough! It lies in the

Why should the people in the four maritime provinces have to pay the cost of a 1,000-mile haul in order to get goods from Ontario and Quebec and have that cost added to every single thing they buy? There is something seriously wrong there. They used to manufacture their own. I do not wish to go into too much detail regarding that matter but I should like to commend the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) for the very fine speech he gave the other day, and several other of the maritime members who have given speeches demanding a fair deal for the maritimes. All honour to these boys. There have to be scores of boys like them coming here from the maritimes and fighting until some intelligence manages to seep into the minds of the people in Ottawa.

The Social Crediters maintain that by a wise use of the financial instruments at the disposal of the Dominion of Canada it is possible for us to set up in the maritime provinces a banking system of their own and a financial system of their own under which they can get loans at a cost such as we in Alberta, after setting up the treasury branch system, were able to get for 5 per cent instead of 8. All we in Ottawa need is to have the will to do it.
Would Ontario and Quebec members rather do that and enable the maritimes to carry on themselves, or would they rather commit their successors or their children and the generations coming after them to a perpetual burden of sending subsidies to those people to enable them to keep themselves? Which would you rather do? Certainly common sense indicates that you would rather give them a financial system of their own under which they can operate effectively.
Similarly with the fiscal policy and trade policy, it is possible for the financial authorities here in Ottawa to enable the people in the maritime provinces to use what the Social Crediters call a compensated discount on the price of their goods, bringing the prices down so low that it will be impossible


for goods from the United States or from Ontario or Quebec to compete with those goods, and thereby bringing the markets in the maritimes to the maritimes, which is exactly one of the fundamental rights of the people. People may say, "I cannot see how that is going to be done." The mere fact that the people now governing in Ottawa cannot see how it can be done indicates that they are unqualified for the positions they fill, because obviously it ought to be possible to render the maritimes capable of that.
I was in New Brunswick recently for some two weeks. I went all over that glorious province and kept my eyes and ears open. I was delighted with the perfect garden of Eden there was down there in New Brunswick. I was delighted over the fine soil there was and I was amazed, and still am somewhat confounded to think about it, that I drove along miles and miles of good New Brunswick roads and saw pastures, which would support the finest kind of cattle and the finest kind of animals and farming operations, raising what they call "cow pasture spruce" there. The mere fact that there exists in that province a set of circumstances under which the people cannot use their resources for the benefit of themselves, indicates that something is dreadfully wrong. The people did not know what it was that was wrong. They had ideas. I do not know whether the government that has just been elected down there knows; perhaps it does. If I talked with a Conservative down there, he said that this cow pasture spruce was growing there because of Liberal mismanagement. If I talked to a Liberal, he said he would explain it so that I would understand. But neither of them got around to doing that job so as to make the matter clear to me.
For this government right here, that situation poses a problem which is inescapable; if they are going to be worthy of the support of the Canadian people, something should be done. They told me in New Brunswick that they were shipping in milk in certain parts and shipping in cheese and butter, right in the presence of the finest pastures a man could put his eyes on. There is something seriously wrong there.
As I said a few minutes ago, I do not intend to go into too much detail except to say that there has been no indication on the part of the government at the present time in Ottawa that they even sense what is wrong down there or that they have any disposition to make it right fundamentally. It is one thing to give a person medicine to relieve pain from which he is suffering; it is another thing to cure the disease which is injuring him. It is the cure for the disease that is

injuring the maritime provinces that we must seek out and apply. That in large measure is a matter of finance.

Before this resolution carries, Mr. Chairman, there is one matter upon which I should like to say a few words. It concerns both the Department of Transport and the Department of Labour. I did indicate to each of the ministers concerned, prior to eleven o'clock this morning, that I would be raising this matter. I note that the Minister of Transport is present and I hope the Minister of Labour will arrive within a minute or two. The question relates to the subject about which I queried the Minister of Transport yesterday. As I have already indicated, it seems to me that it is of concern both to him and to the Minister of Labour. That is one reason for my raising it at this time, when one can talk to two ministers at the same time. My other reason for raising this matter now is that in at least one of the instances of the grievance to which I shall refer something could be done about it if action were taken now because it relates to something that is scheduled to come into effect in a few weeks.
I refer to the fact that the Canadian National Railways seems to be following, far more often it seems to me than is good for labour relations, the practice of letting some of its work out by contract and as a result by-passing certain collective agreements. As hon. members will recall, a number of us complained about this practice last year and the year before with respect to contracts to the R. F. Welch company which had the effect of by-passing collective agreements between the Canadian National Railways and the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees. I understand that matter has been cleared up, in fact that it was cleared up earlier this year. I took the opportunity to indicate to the Minister of Transport that I was pleased that that had been done. It so happened that shortly after I learned that the matter had been cleared up I happened to see Mr. Donald Gordon in another connection and I indicated to him that those of us who had complained about the matter were pleased to know that the union was again being recognized so far as that kind of work was concerned.
However, I am now informed that there are a number of instances in which the Canadian National Railways is doing this same thing. I learned, for example, that at Midland, Ontario, just a few days ago nine carmen's helpers, whose work was covered by a collective agreement between the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees and other transport workers and the Canadian National Railways, lost their jobs because the Canadian National Railways let that work out by contract to a private firm. I understand that similar action has been taken at

Sarnia, Ontario. In both of those cases the work was of the nature of cleaning freight cars, installing car doors and so on. I understand that at Sarnia the rate of pay under the collective agreement was $1.23 and a fraction per hour, but that the employees who enjoyed that wage under a collective agreement are getting only $1 an hour from the private firm to which this work has been let out by contract.
I am told that at the new express building built recently in Toronto the cleaning work has been contracted out at rates below those provided for in collective agreements covering such work. I have other instances before me of various places in Ontario and Quebec where this has been done, and it does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that the railway is doing in this instance precisely what was done previously with respect to the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees. I would hope that the railway, which apparently came to its senses in that other instance, will realize that this is a practice which is highly injurious to labour-management relations and should be brought to a halt right away.
Yesterday, in my question to the Minister of Transport, I asked him also if he would look into the situation that is developing in connection with the restaurant in the union station at Toronto. This is a place with which most of us probably are quite familiar. I would point out that for many years that restaurant has been operated by the Toronto Terminals Railway Company. According to my information, the Toronto Terminals Railway Company is incorporated under Canadian law and is owned jointly by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I find that amongst the directors of the Toronto Terminals Railway Company are such persons as Donald Gordon, N. R. Crump and others from the two railways. I find also that the officers include Donald Gordon, W. A. Mather, R. H. Tarr, and others connected with the two railways. In other words, it is quite clear that the Toronto Terminals Railway Company is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, which is owned by them for the purpose of operating the union station and providing the services at that union station.
However, the employees in the restaurant at the union station in Toronto, whose working conditions have thus far been governed by a collective agreement between the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees and other transport workers and the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, have been notified that their employment will terminate

on August 31. As a matter of fact, on June 20 the employees of the company working in the restaurant at the union station, Toronto, received this communication which I should like to read:
I am directed to inform you that as from September 1, 1956, the restaurants and news stands in the union station will no longer be operated by this company.
The communication was from the Toronto Terminals Railway Company. I continue:
In the circumstances, I am required to give you notice that your employment with the Toronto Terminals Railway Company will terminate not later than the close of business on August 31, 1956.
It is regretted that at the present time there is no other work with the company which can be offered to you. If you wish it, however, your name will be listed as an applicant for such further suitable employment as might become available.
My information is that waitresses working at the union station iri Toronto are receiving $1 an hour at the present time under a collective agreement between their union and the company. Those waitresses have been told that their jobs end on August 31 because of the contract that is being let. Those same waitresses, so I am informed, have been offered their old jobs back under the new management after August 31 at 60 cents an hour. This is the direct result of this policy of letting work out at contract, namely, that these employees will take a reduction from $1 to 60 cents an hour. Likewise, I am told that short-order cooks working there are receiving $1.37 an hour under the collective agreement, but they have been offered 70 cents an hour by the company that is to take over that work.
Now, the Minister of Transport indicated yesterday, when I asked him a question on the orders of the day, that the Toronto Terminals Railway Company is not a railway coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport; but I point out, Mr. Chairman, that it is a company owned by the two major railways in this country, and I point out also that the labour relations of that company are under federal jurisdiction and that the contract referred to which provides the wages I have indicated is a contract under the provisions of the federal Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is a pattern that is a serious one and that every effort should be made to prevent it being continued. Certainly, it is inimical to good labour-management relations to have a company like the Canadian National Railways, or any of its subsidiaries, entering into collective agreements with trade unions and then

undercutting, by-passing, nullifying those contracts by letting work out, as seems to be done in these cases.
As a matter of fact, I have in my hand a copy of an ILO news service release, which is dated April 16, 1956, press release 56/23, having to do with contract labour. This happens to relate to contract labour in the petroleum industry, but I draw attention to the fact that this news release points out that the international labour organization looks with disfavour on letting out work by contract and, as a result, getting around collective agreements. This news release calls for action by government to prevent employers getting around the rights of the union by letting out work on a contract basis. The document also indicates conditions that make possible sound relations and emphasizes the fact that collective agreements should be recognized and their spirit should not be broken, as is being done in this case.
I would point out that this release to which I have referred, while put out by the ILO news service, indicates that 15 countries took part in the session that discussed this matter. Remember that government, labour and management are all represented in the ILO. One of the 15 countries which took part in this discussion was Canada. I am sure that the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour agree with me that collective agreements should not be by-passed in this way, and toward that end I hope that either one or both of these ministers, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour, will get in touch with the management of the Canadian National Railways and, if necessary, with the management of the Toronto Terminals Railway Company and see to it that as the matter was corrected, at least so I am informed, in the case of the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees, it will also be corrected in this case and that this practice will not be further extended.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take one or two minutes to reply to the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He was kind enough this morning privately to supplement the information which was contained in his question yesterday. Before I come to it I would like to say this with regard to the question he asked yesterday, which was as to whether I was aware that the Canadian National Railways is again letting out to private contractors some of its work normally covered by union agreements, and would I look into this practice of by-passing collective agreements. I want to say that I immediately communicated with the management of the railway and, on the information that I was able to

give them by reading the question, they were quite unable to identify the situation to which the hon. member had referred yesterday. This morning the hon. member was good enough to mention specifically these cases which do not fall within the scope of the Welch contract to which he has referred and as to which there has been discussion in the select committee on railways and shipping owned and operated by the government.
I would like to tell the members of the committee, Mr. Chairman, that so far as the examples he has just mentioned are concerned, my consultation with the railway management has been very hasty in view of the short time that has been available, but with regard to the situation at Sarnia I would like to point out that the contract to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred was entered into in May, 1955, not May of this year, and it was a contract entered into with an outside firm for the cleaning of the interior of box cars. There were six labourers and two helpers formerly employed by the railway who were affected by this change. In the case of Midland, the contract was entered into quite recently and, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, it is of a similar character. This affected some 17 railway employees, consisting of 7 car helpers and 10 labourers. One of the seven car helpers had seniority rights from 1947 and another from 1952. These two have been placed in other railway employment. The others were new employees of the railway. I have not been able to get information about the situation in Limoilou, Quebec, but I take it the situation is somewhat similar there to that which exists at Sarnia and Midland. The management have taken some trouble in their communications with me to stress the fact that no complaints whatever have been received from the unions with regard to the arrangements at these points. I think, however, it has always been understood, though I have not read the collective labour agreement between the railway and its employees, that the company reserves the right to have work done on contract when it is demonstrated that this method is more efficient and less costly. Apparently, substantial economies have been effected at Sarnia over the past year. And, Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult, having regard to the obligations which rest upon the railway, to believe that it would be proper for me to intervene and to try to exert pressure on the management to do something that in their judgment ought not to be done. It seems to me we can only obtain the best management and operation of the Canadian National Railway system when management remains free to run the system to the best

advantage so as to procure the best results for the employees and for the public whom they intend to serve. I do not think it is in the interests, either of the employees or of the public, and therefore of the system itself, that they should be restricted to following the same pattern that they have always followed or that they should not be free, when the economics make it more desirable, to do by contract work that perhaps formerly was done by individual employees.
The hon. member referred to the situation in the station restaurant in Toronto. My recollection of the circumstances is the railway company decided that instead of running the restaurant themselves it would be run by a contractor, someone who tendered for the concession. I think the changes of employment are due exactly to the change in that operation.
I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is not seeking to imply that the company should do everything in connection with the system itself and that under no circumstances should outside firms be asked to do by contract such operations as running restaurants and newsstands and so on. I do not think that is the hon. member's intention but I think the management should remain free to do what it considers to be good management of the system property.
There is just one final comment I would like to make. I do not know whether it was the intention of the hon. member to do so but there was an implication that the Canadian National Railways was trying to get around or by-pass the collective labour agreements. I do not believe the circumstances would justify that assertion. My experience with the management of the railway is that when it makes a contract it respects it faithfully and I am sure that is what has been done in this case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for the interest he has taken in this matter as indicated by the fact that he has been in touch with the management of the Canadian National Railways. There are just one or two comments I would like to make.
I am sorry that the Minister of Labour was not able to be here when I made my earlier remarks but I am glad he is in the house now and perhaps he has been informed as to what I had to say.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Labour cannot be unconcerned about the fact that the result of the changes we have been discussing has been that a large number of employees will receive a lower wage than they were getting before. I do not think the Minister of Labour can take without concern the suggestion of the
Interim Supply
Minister of Transport that the management of the Canadian National Railways should be left free to make its own arrangements and that the government should not intervene when the result is that certain people who were formerly making $1.37 an hour are reduced to 70 cents and others formerly making $1 an hour are reduced to 60 cents. The Minister of Labour must be concerned about good labour management relations but certainly this practice hardly comes under that category.
I feel, too, that the Minister of Transport should also be concerned about this matter from the standpoint of the efficient operation of the railway. The minister seems to think if the railway runs its operations more economically than under a previous arrangement that that is good management, but I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if the employees of the railway get the fear that this kind of thing is going to be extended, if the dining car employees become afraid that what can be done to the restaurant employees in Toronto can also be done on the dining cars, it is not going to help much so far as the morale of the employees is concerned and it will affect the running of the railway.
Surely a very integral part of the operation of the railway, in addition to the balance sheets of receipts and expenditures, is the question of the morale of the employees. I strongly urge that this kind of thing is not good for the morale either of the employees whom it directly affects or those who are afraid they might be next on the list.
It has been suggested by the Minister of Transport that he should not be asked to intervene in connection with this matter. I feel very strongly that both he and the Minister of Labour should look into this matter and should make it clear to the C.N.R. that employee conditions are an integral and important part of the operation of the Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret that owing to another meeting I was not in the house when this discussion began but I think I know the gist of the discussion.
I can tell my hon. friend that as Minister of Labour I have not had direct representation from the employees with regard to the matter under discussion this afternoon. Not since the two parties agreed to work out their general agreements on the basis of conciliation board reports have I had any formal representations from the unions or the employees, and consequently I am not in a position to make any statement as to what should or should not be done concerning the matter in hand.

Interim Supply

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

What I was referring to this afternoon was another instance or several other instances so far as another union was concerned, namely the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees and other transport workers. I am sure that as the minister interested himself when representations were made by the other union, if representations come from this union he will give the matter his attention.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 85. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $6,145,727.

On Friday, June 29, the
minister made some remarks, as recorded on page 5520 of Hansard, concerning a gun contract with Sorel Industries Limited of Sorel, Quebec. I should like to read a few paragraphs of the remarks he made at that time in this connection, beginning at the third line on page 5520:
In this connection, I should like to refer briefly to the contracts for the three-inch 50 calibre antiaircraft guns to which reference was made in the report of the Auditor General for the last fiscal year. These contracts were carried out by Sorel Industries Limited in its gun plant at Sorel, Quebec, on behalf of the United States and Canadian governments, and the difference of some $112,000 each in the cost to the two governments provides a good example of the heavy expense of re-establishing a facility to do this type of work.
Apart from minor extras for special equipment required by the Canadian navy, the difference in price was accounted for mainly by three items of expenditure which were considered to apply to Canadian account only, inasmuch as they related to the re-establishment of Canada's only facility for the production of heavy guns urgently required by the armed services at the outbreak of the Korean war. These were plant and staff house rehabilitation expenses totalling some $908,000, or $19,900 per gun; plant maintenance costs, covering partial compensation for the expense of retaining this highly specialized gun facility (which had little or no economic commercial use) during the period from 1945 to 1950, amounting to $35,074 per mount; and the pre-production and learning expenses amounting to $33,158 per gun. These figures represent general overhead costs of the first year's operations which could not properly be absorbed in the relatively small volume of production during that period, bearing in mind that the plant had to be re-activated and staffed from a virtual shutdown condition.
I should like to say a few words about these three items of expenditure to which

the minister referred. He had mentioned one, the staff house rehabilitation expenses, amounting to some $908,000. In the other two items he mentioned he gave figures as costs per gun. I should like to summarize those as the actual amount of dollars spent. The three items are: for pre-production and learning, $1,338,436; the cost of plant and staff house rehabilitation, $908,453; and portion of settlement with contractor to compensate for maintaining this highly specialized facility, $1,525,428. That comes to a total amount of $3,772,317.
I should like to refer to another item in connection with this contract. The actual profit, which was based on the 7 per cent figure, on the United States guns was $16,295 per mount and with 180 guns that amounts to $2,933,100. The Canadian profit per gun, owing to extra parts and so on, and as a consequence of the 7 per cent figure being somewhat higher, was $18,259. There were 46 guns under this contract, and that comes to a total of $839,914. Adding those two profit figures together, we come to a total, on the 7 per cent profit basis, of $3,773,014.
I should like to refer back for a minute to these three items which the minister mentioned as being peculiar to the Canadian guns. That figure is $3,772,317. It may be only coincidence, but it looks as though they are very similar amounts, and in the calculation here one would almost suspect that the contract might well have been considered on a 14 per cent basis, then cutting out half of it to put against the Canadian guns and splitting the other on a 7 per cent basis.
I mentioned these three items and I should like to say a few words about the third item particularly, the portion of settlement with the contractor to compensate for maintaining this highly specialized facility. That amounts to $1,525,428. Possibly we should go back and review briefly the history of plant as it existed at that moment.
In 1945 Sorel Industries Limited was relieved of any further armament orders relating to the second world war. The company was advised not to keep open in anticipation of further government orders for guns. Then came 1950 and Korea. Negotiations between the Department of Defence Production and Sorel Industries were reopened. Actual figures were agreed upon in March 1955, and a 7 per cent profit figure, which totalled $3,773,014, was determined, and also the total for these three items of $3,772,317.
Between 1945 and 1950, I should say, Sorel Industries operated as any other commercial
Supply-Defence Production corporation doing peacetime business without any hopes of further armament orders. They had been led not to expect any more.
I should like to review briefly the wording of this third portion of the expenditure of $3,772,317. The portion of settlement with the contractor to compensate for maintaining this highly specialized facility cannot mean to me anything other than compensation for loss of profits in the period 1945 to 1950. This sum of $1,525,428 was on this one contract only. The total amount paid to Sorel Industries Limited under this pretext was based on $80,000 per month for three years and came to a grand total of $2,880,000.
I feel that the company was paid sufficient mark-up on their contracts when they received a 7 per cent profit plus pre-production and learning expenses of $1,338,000-odd and the cost of plant and staff house rehabilitation amounting to $908,453. I cannot understand why they should be reimbursed for losses during the period from 1945 to 1950 when they had been told that they would be entirely on their own and not to expect any further government contracts. I have never heard of a similar contract where such a clause was inserted to cover a period such as this when the company was on its own operating as a private commercial business, and to me, sir, it appears to be an unjustified handout to the company of $2,880,000 of public money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Has the minister nothing to say about the matter raised by the hon. member for Perth?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The matter was discussed in a committee of the house of which I think my hon. friend was a member and I cannot believe that there was any fact that was not placed before that committee. Sorel Industries have the only heavy gun plant that we have in the country. It was closed down in 1945. Very valuable machinery was available there and when it was quite obvious that we would require guns for the Korean crisis we of course were anxious to make an arrangement with Sorel that the machinery would be kept intact for that purpose.
The owners of Sorel Industries took the view that as they had a plant that had to be kept closed between wars and opened during war they were entitled to a profit based on that situation. We took the view that perhaps they had some claim not for any profit between wars but to recover some of the dead loss which must be incurred in keeping a plant like that idle and keeping the machinery up as must be done if we are going to have the machinery when it is needed.

Supply-Defence Production
A settlement was made on the basis that we took, I think, one-half the loss that had been incurred in keeping the plant closed and we told them that as regards any work they would do in war they would get the same rate of profit that any other contractor would get regardless of the fact that the plant is only called upon in wartime. That was a decision made after a good deal of consultation. My officers made the recommendation and after examination I concurred. I think it was a reasonable settlement of the cost of maintaining a highly specialized plant for a purpose that is essential in war but has no place in peacetime. If there is any mistake involved I will take full responsibility for it. If there is good judgment I think I am entitled to the credit.

There is one point I should like to stress. The plant had been told that in the period following the end of the 1945 hostilities there would be no further armament orders and as a consequence I would feel that they should be on their own responsibility entirely as to what happened in that peacetime period up until further contracts were going to be negotiated.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a privately owned plant and we did not agree to buy anything in 1945. We said that we did not expect any further call for heavy equipment and that as far as we were concerned they could close the plant. Nevertheless, as owners of a private plant that had to be used in the Korean emergency I think you will agree they were under no compulsion to make guns for us at 7.2 per cent or whatever the percentage was of the rate of profit. The arrangement was made to work out something that would be fair and so that we would not have to make any different profit arrangement for the use of that plant. After all, I am accused by the opposition of wielding a big stick on industry. In fact we negotiate fairly with industry and I think we did so in this case.

Following that one step
further, I have nothing to say about the minister's wielding a big stick but I do have this to say. The minister indicates that when these contracts were entered into in 1950 the company did not have to make these guns at a 7 per cent profit figure. If they had been losing money, as is indicated, for the previous five years I would think they would be most happy to take a contract at a 7 per cent profit figure. Their straight profit figure aside from rehabilitation expenses and so on was $3,773,000 on this one contract only and there were many subsequent contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If my hon. friend had a plant worth $25 million by anyone's estimate and it was his plant and he could do what he liked with it I doubt very much if he would keep it idle for five years, stand the cost of maintaining a $25 million plant in idleness and then be willing to take a contract at 7-2 per cent. I think he would have said: "That highly specialized machinery is now valuable and I had better sell it and cash in on some of the value." After all, we must be practical about these things. This idea that somebody must be glad to do something depends on a little wider consideration than my hon. friend gives it.
I do not agree with that. I think I am as practical minded as the minister. In fact, I think in some ways I am probably more so.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In a small way.

I am more money conscious and I would query, as I am doing, this $2,880,000 which has been given to Sorel Industries and which appears to me to be a handout for loss of profits from 1945 to 1950 when they had been told to close up and expect no more government orders.

Perhaps it would help to clarify the matter to some extent if the minister would tell the committee whether this company received any capital assistance either before or after 1945 and, if so, in what amounts and on what terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They did obtain some capital assistance in 1951 for some specialized machinery required for the manufacture of the 3 inch 50 calibre gun. The capital assistance took the form of machinery that was purchased by the government, installed in the plant and remained the property of the government. It was no handout to the company. It was simply installing certain specialized machines there that were required to carry out the contract.

Perhaps the minister could supplement his answer by giving us the figures as to the amount of capital assistance given and on what terms. He states that machinery was supplied and that it is still the property of the government. In the meantime the company has had the use of the machinery and it was instrumental in providing the profit to which my hon. friend refers. What consideration has the government received in return for supplying the machinery? Obviously if it has been used by the company since 1951 the government is certainly entitled to some consideration for having supplied the

machinery. I should like to know in what amount and on what terms this machinery was supplied.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Machinery to the value of about $6 [DOT] 5 million was installed. I may say that is in addition to about $20 million odd of machinery that was in the plant prior to that time.
Was that all done in 1951?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: 1951 and thereafter.

The other part of my question was, on what basis was the $6-5 million of machinery supplied and on what terms? Was that simply a form of subsidy on the part of the government to the company or was there some consideration so far as the government is concerned? Is the company under any obligation so far as the $6-5 million is concerned or can that be considered a subsidy to that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. It is not
a subsidy at all. The government bought that machinery and it was installed in the plant. It is the property of the federal government. Whether any of it has been taken out as yet, I cannot say; but it will be taken out and probably installed in the arsenal at some time or other when we decide that we are not likely to need this machinery any more at Sorel. It is painted a different colour than the other machinery. It is listed in the government inventory and it belongs to the government.
On the basis of that answer, there seems to be something still missing. The company has had the use of this machinery now for five years. It was installed in 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Exclusively on government work.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The company is not allowed to use it on any private work.

That is understood; but on government work for which they were paid a profit of approximately 17-2 per -cent. On the basis of ordinary depreciation, if the government were to claim that machinery now, it would be worth approximately $2 million. What does the government get out of the companies having the use of their machinery for five years? Do they get no consideration at all? It is not enough to say that they were working on government contracts. They were working on contracts for which they were paid a profit, and I would say it was a very adequate profit at that. Does that mean that
Supply-Defence Production the government puts this machinery into a privately owned plant for five years where it depreciates, or is used for that period? The fact that the government owns it at the end of the five years does not mean much, because it will be practically worthless as time goes on. Does that mean that the amount of depreciation on that machinery over a five year period is a direct subsidy to the company? I can see it from no other point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Considering the fact that all the work being done was work for which the department was paying, it was rather a subsidy to the government. It would have been an additional cost had the machinery been installed by the company. The depreciation would have been paid that way and the contractor's profit would have been that much greater. At least the depreciation allowance would have entered into the calculation of profits, as depreciation is an item we must allow as a cost. We followed the usual practice in work of this kind. The United States government are quite happy about the arrangements which were made there. They paid, of course, for most of the work in Sorel. They had the larger part of the production. The arrangement was one that seemed to them to be a reasonable arrangement, and, as far as I know, no one is complaining except my hon. friend. It seems to me that when this is threshed out in the committee and the evidence is given there-I was not present but everyone else was-if committees are going to be used to collect evidence to use against the minister in the house, I do not think committees serve a very useful purpose in this house.
I think that is why it would be useful. That is an argument for having the committees.
That would be an argument for having the committees.

I think that is a most unfair statement and in my opinion a most unparliamentary one. Certainly if a committee is set up in order to obtain information, and if the information indicates that either the minister or the government used poor judgment in connection with these contracts, the members of that committee or any other member of the house should not feel at all backward about using the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If the committee comes to the conclusion that there is something wrong or that there has been waste, surely it is the duty of the committee to make a finding of that kind and report it to

Supply-Defence Production the house. Then we will all be on even terms. But for individual members of the committee to go in there to pick up special facts and information that I cannot get without a good deal of study, and throw bits of information at me and expect me to know the answers, is a procedure which I think is a little bit unreasonable if they are used for that purpose. Why did not the hon. member raise the point in the committee and ask the committee to make a finding in this case?

I should like to say that this information I had presented has come from the committee and it has come from the minister's deputy. We asked questions and we received answers. I am convinced that the information that I have presented is correct, as represented by those answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That may be so.
But if there was something wrong, why did my hon. friend not move that the committee find that there was waste of government funds and move that a report be presented to that effect? Did my hon. friend move that in committee?
I would suggest that the committee tell the chairman of the committee to call a meeting of the committee and report.

The minister seems to have a most peculiar idea of the functions of a committee. He seems to think it should be for the purpose of white-washing the minister and the government and that, if it does not do so, it has been a failure as a committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; quite the reverse. If the committee finds that there is something wrong, it is the duty of the committee so to report to the house.
The committee so far has had no opportunity to report. We have not had a meeting since the meeting we had in connection with this gun contract, as a matter of fact.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: There have been no requests for a meeting of the committee from you or from anybody else.

To come back to this same matter, the minister says that we must be practical about these things. I agree that we must be practical. But in this particular case it seems to me we have an example of being impractical and improvident as far as the government is concerned.
