It is a very peculiar situation, I think, when you have a plant which the government told Sorel Industries that they should turn over to some civilian use or not keep in operation as a gun plant in 1945. As a matter of fact,
(Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).]
that was the evidence we had in the committee. The evidence also was to the effect, or at least there was an intimation, that Sorel Industries attempted to put some sort of civilian enterprise into it but failed to do so. Then in 1950, when there just happens to be some opportunity to manufacture guns, the government then goes to this plant and agrees to pay it a total of $2,880,000 to cover the costs of that business or of that plant standing idle for several years. The thing is just a ridiculous situation. As far as I can see, the government or the taxpayer had no responsibility whatever to reimburse Sorel Industries for whatever loss they may have experienced through having that plant sitting there and maintaining it for five years. Undoubtedly Sorel Industries made plenty of profit out of the plant during the war to begin with. I do not know who built the plant. Probably the government advanced the money or a good part of it for the building of that plant to start with.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is not true. The plant was built as a privately owned plant.
Yes, but did they not get capital assistance and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Later on they did.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
But in the end
they bought from the government all the assets that the government had there and paid for them in cash.

In any event you have a plant there which had got capital assistance with respect to the building of it in the first instance; and they made sufficient profit out of what they manufactured in it during the war to pay for it. Then five years later the taxpayer of this country is called upon to pay $2,880,000 to this company because the plant has been sitting there for five years after they had been told not to keep it sitting there as far as expecting any future contracts is concerned. The thing is just a ridiculous situation. As I say, I think it is an extremely improvident deal as far as the Canadian taxpayer is concerned.
In addition to that, this company got assistance of $908,000 for the cost of rehabilitating shops and staff houses and it got an amount of $1,338,000 approximately for the cost of making ready to resume production after this long shut-down, including cost of recruiting this labour, training this labour and so on. Therefore, all told, that company is being paid in cash over $5 million in order to make these guns. Now they are in a position that they are making certain other guns, I believe they are 105 millimeter guns.

But over $5 million in cash was being paid. In addition to that, as was indicated by the answers given to the hon. member for Dawson, the government has a great deal of machinery, upwards of $2 million worth, in there which they are making use of. In other words, the company has had extremely large grants and assistance from the dominion government.
In addition to that, they are given seven per cent profit on what they produced in that time. As a result of this information that we were given, it is very easy to see why the Canadian naval guns which were secured from them cost $112,000 each more than did the guns which went to the United States. Naturally the United States government would not put up money for payments of that kind because it is so unreasonable. I imagine that the United States government would never agree to making a share of these payments aggregating all told, as I say, over $3,770,000 on this one particular contract, plus another $1,300,000 so far as future contracts are concerned, and at the same time making loans on machinery.
In addition to these particular payments to cover the cost of the plant sitting idle from 1940 to 1945, I should like to know something more about this business of the cost of rehabilitating the shops and staff houses, including considerable plant machinery. When we were considering this matter in committee I asked how much of that was for rehabilitating these staff houses. I was told it was something in excess of $200,000. I said at that time, and I will say again, that it seems to me there is absolutely no justification for the taxpayers' money being used to rehabilitate or repair certain staff houses which are used by employees hired by this company. Questions were asked as to how much rent they paid for these houses or whether they paid any rent for them. It developed that they were sort of single men's dwelling places more than anything else; in other words, something in the nature of barracks.
We find that what these people paid for these staff houses was as follows: In 1951- this is for room and board-they paid $16 per week; 1952, $17; 1953, $16; 1954, $18. In other words, this $200,000 was given as a further subsidy to this company which enabled them to house their employees at much less cost than would have been the case if they had had to compete with other people building housing at commercial rates. In connection with this housing, I should like to ask the minister who built those houses in the first place? When were they built and who paid for them? I should like to know, in other words, whether the government paid for those houses to begin with?
Supply-Defence Production

Before the minister answers I think I ought to set the record straight concerning some of the remarks the hon. member for Calgary North has just made. In my capacity as chairman of the public accounts committee I think I should point out to the house that when my hon. friend said he was surprised at the difference of $112,000 in the case of the United States guns-
I did not say I was surprised.
You said you did not like it.
I do not like it, but I am not surprised.

In any case, you certainly criticized it, and gave the impression that it had not been explained. I think the house should know that the difference in cost between these guns was analysed, was placed before the committee and was examined in detail by the committee. I think we are entitled to take it for granted that the committee was satisfied, because the draft report of the committee has been submitted to the steering committee of the public accounts committee, and has been approved by the steering committee of which the hon. member for Calgary North is a member; and the report does not blame the government in any way for any of the matters that were looked into and that came to light in connection with this contract for the guns.
It was also said that we have not had a meeting of the committee lately. As I said before, we had a meeting of the steering committee the day before yesterday and a meeting of the committtee is called for tomorrow to have the whole committee approve a report that has already been approved by the steering committee. I felt it was necessary to put these facts on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I suspected that, but I did not know it.

In reply to that I should like to say that we asked to have this particular gun contract investigated by the public accounts committee not very long after the committee had started to sit, I think at about the second or third meeting, as the result of one of the paragraphs in the Auditor General's report. This was some months ago. Eventually, after a long delay during which there had not been any meetings of the public accounts committee and after I got in contact with the chairman of the committee, we finally had a meeting on July 5, at which we had evidence in connection with this particular contract. The presumption was, when we left that meeting,

Supply-Defence Production that we were going to have a further meeting, which has never been held. As a matter of fact-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: It was never asked for.
It was asked for at that time. We went away with the presumption we were going to have a further meeting. In any event, certain questions which were-
Will the hon. member permit a question?
-asked have never been answered.

Will you show me in the record of the committee where you asked for another meeting? You never did ask for another meeting. While I am putting the record straight, may I say that when you or any other member of the committee asked for a meeting it was always granted.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I am afraid that perhaps through my own fault we are getting this committee into a situation which should not be allowed. The subject which was brought up for discussion by the hon. member for Perth, of course, is a legitimate subject for discussion under defence production estimates. The Department of Defence Production estimates were not referred to a committee; therefore the fact that a discussion took place in the public accounts committee does not in any way prevent this committee now from discussing it.
The agenda committee of the public accounts committee has not submitted its report, and a discussion of its proceedings at this time is definitely out of order. I think it is obvious that I permitted the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine and the hon. member for Calgary North to go further than I should. We are now in the process of discussing not the estimates of the Department of Defence Production, but the conduct of the committee on public accounts. I hope the statements made by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine and the hon. member for Calgary North have been made and replied to by each of them to such an extent that we may consider the matter closed.
I am not ruling out of order any discussion about a particular gun contract which was let by defence production, but I am going to ask hon. members not to discuss the conduct of the committee on public accounts or its agenda committee until such time as it makes its report, which I believe is not very far off.

I should like, if I may, to say that at the very end of this day's proceedings to which the chairman of the public


accounts committee, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine, referred, and after we had left these questions which you yourself will remember had not been answered, the chairman said:
We shall adjourn to the call of the chair. It remains for me to thank Mr. Golden and his officials who have been called to give us this information.
Now, I will get the required information from the department concerned, namely-
And so on. I believe the only thing anyone could take from that was that there was a further meeting of the committee to be held in order to receive those answers and get this further information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: That is simply the normal procedure for the chairman of any committee.
Not that another meeting would be held to get further information, but that another meeting would be held to draft our report and finish it.
I think no one could take any other meaning from it than the one I took, that we would have a further meeting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You are the only one who did.
I wonder if the minister could answer those questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: The profit would have been 14 per cent if you added in these other items.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, what are they? What do the other items amount to?
On this particular contract the other items amount to $3,772,316?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Then there is this further amount of $1,300,000 odd which they have been given in addition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was cost; it was not profit.

These were not costs. This was the amount which was paid to them just because they had the plant sitting there for the five years from 1945 to 1950 to begin with, and it is the cost of rehabilitating those staff houses and other things along that line, which I can see no justification for the Canadian taxpayer paying. It was the cost, as it is outlined here, of making ready to resume production. Therefore in the three items the total is $3,772,000 odd. If you add that to the 7-2 per cent profit they were given it brings it up to a profit of more than 14 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The cost of preparing a plant for production is preproduction cost; it is not a profit. It is paying for the cost of assembling and training the men. How you can figure that to be a profit I am sure I do not know. My hon. friend is used to army life and I am used to production, but I never heard of production costs of that kind described as profit.
It sounds like gravy.

As far as that particular item is concerned, or part of it, you cannot consider it as profit; but I think there is no doubt at all that this $1,500,000 odd is just an extra profit and, as a matter of fact, I think that was brought out in evidence before the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Not at all.

Really what it came down to was an extra profit. Similarly, this amount which was given for rehabilitating staff houses cannot be looked upon as anything else but an extra profit. It is just a way of concealing profits, as far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Who got the
profit?
So far as all these items are concerned-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Who got the profit in rehabilitating the staff houses?

Sorel Industries got it, of course. Who else got it? The money was paid over to them. If it had not been paid by the taxpayer they would have had to pay it themselves. As far as this $1,500,000 is concerned that they were given, they were given it just because they had the plant sitting there. They had failed, after having been told by the government to keep the plant sitting waiting for more munitions orders, and so forth, to establish any ordinary industry in it; and as a result of their
Supply-Defence Production failure to establish ordinary industry in it, which most other people were able to do, they were then paid $2,880,000 in 1950 and subsequently because they had failed to establish any ordinary industry in that plant.

Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the public accounts committee and therefore do not intend to debate the proceedings in that committee; but I am interested in a contradiction in statements when I find it.
This afternoon the minister has expounded a most interesting theory as to the purposes which committees of this house are intended and are not intended to serve. He has said that if committees of this house are to be used to gather together information to be brought into this house and used to embarrass the minister on his estimates, then we should take another look at these committees, in effect, and decide whether we ought to have committees at all because it is a wrong use to make of them. I am not surprised at a statement like that coming from the minister, because it is quite in keeping with his whole political philosophy.
But here again this afternoon we have an interesting example of the application of the minister's political theory in that regard. This afternoon the minister was asked for an explanation of a figure which aggregates $2,880,000 which was paid as a profit, and is figured as a profit. The explanation given by the minister to this committee this afternoon was that this was paid to Sorel Industries Limited because that company was asked to keep its plant in idleness but available for military production if required. Now, the basis on which the minister sought to establish the payment-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is not true. Your statement is not correct.
Mr. Chairman, that is what the minister said, if the record stands as the minister made his statement this afternoon. If that were the fact-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is not the fact.
-the payment made to the company, of course, would be justified if they were asked to keep their plant in idleness and not to put" it to some other use.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The evidence is just the opposite.
Payments made to them for that purpose would be proper if the payments were reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My hon. friend is lost.

Supply-Defence Production
Mr. Chairman, are we going to have any order and is the minister going to respect the rules of the house, or is he going to break them all? Just sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Who was it that was thrown out of this house?
The minister does not pay any attention to the rules of this house. He is at it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Who was it that was thrown out?

I said if that plant had been kept in idleness at the request of the government in order that the plant and its machinery would be available to be thrown into war production, or defence production, when required, it would be only proper that the company should be compensated for it, if the amount was reasonable, and that is the basis -I call upon hon. members to witness what was said-that is the basis upon which the minister this afternoon sought to justify the payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-
What is the fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: On a question of privilege-
The fact is, as we have been informed-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No such statement was made, and the record will not show it. My hon. friend can repeat it as loudly as he likes, and let him accuse me of breaking the rules.
It is perfectly typical for the minister to try to smuggle in a speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps
we ought to have a little order. The Minister of Defence Production rose on a point of order which actually was, I take it, for the purpose of denying the accuracy of a statement made by the hon. member for Eglinton. I would suggest that the hon. member for Eglinton complete his remarks and the Minister of Defence Production will then have ample opportunity to reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I ask you a
question, sir? Are we still on item No. 1?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We are still on item No. 85, which is departmental administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
What are we going to do when we get to item No. 2, which is the item under which this matter could more properly be discussed?
IMr. Howe (Port Arthur).]

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think there is a lot of merit in that, but I just do not see how I can start at ten minutes to four to say that this discussion should have been on another item when it has been going on since about 2.30. Perhaps it would suit everybody's convenience and promote efficiency if we tried to complete discussion of this particular incident on this particular item, as it is now perhaps nearly completed anyway. The hon. member for Eglinton.

On the point of order the minister brought up, I would have been glad to discuss this matter on item 87, but I reckoned on item 87 it would have been out of order and the minister would have said it was out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I point out to the
hon. member for Calgary North that we have decided the discussion is to continue on item 85. The hon. member for Eglinton.

Mr. Chairman, the only basis upon which the minister could have justified this payment of $2,880,000 to this company as profit would have been if the company had been asked to retain that plant and hold it available for government use. On no other basis could any such payment be justified by the minister, or by anyone else. But what do we find to be the fact? The fact, as disclosed by his deputy minister, is that the company was advised in 1945 not to keep the plant open. The statement was quite clear that the company was told in 1945, "don't look to the government. We are not telling you to hold that plant available to us; on the contrary, we are telling you not to keep your plant open".
Therefore the company evidently quite clearly was told at that time, "So far as that plant is concerned, you are on your own; you are warned. Do the best you can with it, but don't look to the government". But five years later what happens? At that time the government required the production of this plant for war purposes, and it was not sufficient at that time to provide the company with the cost of opening up the plant. No one would question proper costs of starting the plant up again for war production.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary North does.

No; that is a very different thing. He is not challenging the minister's inclusion in these costs of production of things that were quite properly so classified. I am just stating the facts. It is perfectly clear. The minister can not come back and

change what has been said already in this discussion this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary North.
But, sir, here we are dealing with a payment the government makes as profit, retroactive for the whole period of five years from 1945 to 1950, a period during which this company has been warned not to look to the government, that they were on their own. They had been told not to keep their plant open; yet when 1950 comes the government is not satisfied just to pay a fair amount to this company to get the plant in operation at that point. They say in an outburst of extraordinary generosity-perhaps not too extraordinary for this government, but an outburst that most taxpayers in this country would regard as extremely extraordinary and quite indefensible-to that plant, "Well, we will go back and say that we told you to look after yourselves for this five-year period, but we will now hand out $2,880,000 of the money of the taxpayers of this country as a payment equivalent to the profit you would have made if you kept that plant open."
The government not only did not ask them to keep the plant open but told them at that time not to keep the plant open for war purposes or for government purposes; yet here is a juicy sum of $2,880,000 handed out in 1950, five years later, apparently to give this company something that was not earned. Now, the minister drove some kind of bargain with this company-*

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: A tough bargain.

-and the terms of the bargain included a payment which in my submission, based on what we have heard here this afternoon was a highly improper and unjustifiable payment, a payment made retroactively to give this company profit for five years for this plant. Whether it was sitting idle or whether it was in use does not matter, because it was not in use for the government and it was not kept in idleness at the government's request. Here we have the statement of the deputy minister of this department that this company was told in 1945 not to keep the plant open; yet they were paid $2,880,000 in 1950 for the consideration that they kept the plant open.
We have had, I think, a very telling example this afternoon of the benefit of having committees of this house do a little scouting, and particularly the benefit of having a committee do some scouting around this department.
When I spoke on June 29 in the opening discussion on the estimates of this department I urged that there should be a review in a select committee of the operations of this
Supply-Defence Production department. This department has now been in existence for the last five or six years. In the course of that period it has expended $6 billion, and there has not been a select committee which has had an opportunity to make a thorough study of it. It is true that the committee-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Three sessions, three committees.

No, no. Again the parliamentary assistant is just repeating the same erroneous statements he made on June 29. The fact is that we had a committee on defence expenditure. The first year that committee met was before this department got set up and in operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

That is what I said on June 29. The two later years that committee sat no one -can pretend it did more than a bit of scratching on the surface. What we have seen this afternoon, sir, ought to be abundant evidence to satisfy any reasonable person that what is needed is a very detailed review of the administration of this department and of some of the contracts that have been entered into.
At the beginning of this session the Leader of the Opposition asked that the estimates of various departments should be sent to the estimates committee. Those that were sent were of the government's choosing, and we objected to their choosing. We asked that one of the departments at least of this minister should go to that committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You asked for trade and commerce.
Yes, and we would have been glad to have it. It is one for which we asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You did not say so.
We were turned down.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You did not say so.

We were turned down; the government would not accept any request from the opposition as to any department. They made the selection, and it will be left to the hon. members of this house and the public to ask themselves why it is the government wants to pick and choose what departments are to have their estimates and their administration reviewed in detail by committees.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it just so happens this afternoon that because another committee of the house, the public accounts committee, happened to have an opportunity to do a little looking into this particular contract and the

Supply-Defence Production juicy payments that were made to this company in connection with it, that we have had information from the deputy minister of that department to correct the statements made here by the minister this afternoon.
If that information had not been available to us through the committee I suppose we would have been in the position of having statements from the minister to justify this payment on the ground that this plant had been kept in idleness at the request of or for the benefit of the government. We know that is not the fact, and there is no justification for this payment; and I say all credit to those members of the public accounts committee who obtained the facts there and to the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Calgary North who have brought this information to the attention of this committee this afternoon and have established that there was a payment of $2,880,000 which, as the hon. member for Perth said this afternoon, was just a handout.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I have heard my hon. friend distort other situations-*
No, you never have.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -but I think the distortion of this particular matter-
You have never heard me distort the truth; not if you recognize the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -excels his usual distortion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You hand it out; just take it for a change.
Sit still for a while.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member stated that I said in 1945 we asked the company to keep this plant ready for operation. The fact is exactly the opposite.
We know that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was said in the committee and I have said it in the house. I knew it then and of course I know it now.
Why did you try to justify the payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member is trying to sneak in an extra speech just as he accused me of doing.
I asked a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You are the hon. member who was thrown out of the house for butting in.
And you are the man who should be thrown out today-
Get the facts.
-and when I was very improperly suspended on May 25-
Ha, ha.
-by the vote of the majority of this house-[DOT]
Order.
-here is the minister who should have been thrown out if he were not a member of the majority.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. May I remind the committee that we are discussing, or should be, the estimates of the Department of Defence Production and that incidents which have been previously decided by actions of the house are closed so far as this discussion is concerned. May I say to the hon. member for Eglinton, as I said to the minister a short time ago, that the Minister of Defence Production should be permitted to make his statement and an opportunity will be given for reply.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The rules do not apply to the hon. member for Eglinton.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The facts of the matter are that in 1945 we had to decide what facilities outside of those owned by the government we wished to keep active. In the matter of Sorel we looked into that, and it was a very costly affair to keep that plant active. We notified the company that we did not intend to do so. The company were told that they were free to dispose of the equipment and turn the plant over to civilian use. Well, they chose not to do so. The matter was considered and I know they had offers for some of the equipment. Some of the equipment was specialized and some of it was standard, and it was all very valuable. I know they received an offer from another government for the equipment. They came to see me and on my advice they did not accept the offer.
However, we had no obligations to the plant and we would have had no obligations had we never required the plant again. In other words, if the Korean situation had not come along and if we had not been again required to build heavy guns in quantity in this country we had no obligation to the plant.
Then we found in 1950-1949, I guess it was-that we did have a requirement for the plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We did have it; and we naturally went to the company and said, "We need your plant; what arrangements can we make?"
Were there any other companies in the same position that received the same type of reward?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Here is another man. He is the hit and run artist. It is not time for him to hit yet. He had better listen for a while.

I wondered whether
Sorel Industries was the favourite company.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just let me tell you the story. You can make your speech later, after you have picked up a few facts. Your arms will wave-
We are trying to get the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
You don't worry about the truth. However, we came to this point in 1949 or 1950. I do not remember when we decided that we were going to need the plant. However, we said, "We need your plant." They brought us a bill that showed us the cost of maintaining that plant without orders for the intervening period, and they said, "What about that? We shall require a special profit if the plant is to be used for a two or three-year period. If you want to make a long-term arrangement for the use of our plant that is one thing, but do you intend to give any undertaking that at the time these contracts are filled there will be a future for the plant?" We said, "No, we do not think that as part of the defence effort we should undertake to carry as part of our long-range equipment a plant of that size. We want to make an arrangement for the work incidental to the Korean emergency, and we want no continuing obligations."
A good deal of negotiation went on. My officers are familiar with it because they carried on the bulk of it. It was decided that we would pay a portion of the cost that had been involved in carrying on the plant. Incidentally, that was not a profit: it was made up of expenditures that had been made by the company, as indicated by their books. An arrangement was made that having given some compensation for that, we would treat them on the same basis as any other contractor and pay the costs ordinarily allowed for the work performed according to our own formulas of allowable profit.
We had then in hand an order for 48 guns for the Canadian navy. You may say it was not worth starting up a plant of that size to make 48 three-inch 50 calibre guns. Nevertheless it was the policy at that time to make sure that Canada was self-sufficient as far as naval production was concerned, and as
Supply-Defence Production part of that program the navy wished to have those guns manufactured in Canada.
We started up the plant on the theory that we were going to make 48 guns for the Canadian navy. The starting up expenses were based on the Canadian program. Later on we were able to obtain a share of the United States program for the same guns, and from then on we were able to divide our costs over a much greater base. In the end, I think, the situation worked out quite well. We finished up the United States guns to their complete satisfaction. They shared in the costs from the time their contract was entered in the books, and their participation very greatly lowered the overhead on the Canadian part of the project.
The two guns were not exactly the same. The Americans sent up a breech-block made by a special contractor in the United States who made the breech-blocks for all the United States guns. Our own navy wanted their own breech-block, and we had to tool up in Canada to make that breech-block. This accounted for some part of the difference in costs-not a great part, but that was the main physical difference between the two guns.
What we did there is what we would have done had we used a similar plant anywhere else. You say that we put in the bunk-houses. Certainly; when we use a plant that had not been active or had been active on a lower scale we give capital assistance, as we did in this case, to put the facilities in shape to carry out the work that we have for the plant. There was nothing exceptional about the Sorel situation, except that we picked up part of the cost of maintaining the plant and the equipment in the plant in idleness for the intervening five years.
My hon. friend from Eglinton said that it would have been quite all right if we had decided to do that in 1945. We decided not to do it then, but that does not alter the equity of the situation. When we found that we would profit by the fact that the plant had been kept intact, the equity of the situation, and the desirability of putting the plant on all fours with every other plant that had been in use in the interval, as far as the entitlement to profit was concerned, was considered by my officers and myself as a sufficient reason for making a settlement on part of the out of pocket costs of maintaining the plant over the intervening five years.

Now will the minister answer a question? Does the minister confirm the fact that this company was told in 1945 not to keep its plant open as far as the government was concerned?

Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Certainly; I
told them myself and I have never represented otherwise. My hon. friend is the only one that has represented that I said otherwise. I do not know whether I wrote them a letter advising them to that effect, but I told them in any event.
The statement of the minister just now completely obliterates any justification for the payment of $2,800,000.
In your opinion.

The minister, in replying to the hon. member for Eglinton, I think was attempting to represent me as saying something which was not just what I did say. What I was trying to get at here, as far as these two items are concerned, the cost of rehabilitating the shops and staff houses and the cost of making ready, were the amounts which were used for various things. I had said that I could see no justification whatever for the Canadian taxpayer paying $200,000-odd for rehabilitation of these staff houses. I should like the minister to give us a breakdown of this item, and I should like a breakdown of the other item later. I should like a breakdown first of the item $908,450 for rehabilitating shops and staff houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Do you expect me to give it from memory? This is only item 1.
The minister has his officials here, and possibly they could provide that for him. Perhaps he is not showing rnough confidence in them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They tell me they do not have it. However, we shall get it as soon as we can and supply it to my hon. friend.

The minister gave some
figures on the Sorel contract which are interesting. If I heard him correctly, he stated that this company has manufactured approximately $100 million worth of guns over a period of time-I did not catch the period-and for that they received a profit of approximately $7 [DOT] 2 million or 7-2 per cent. Let us take the period from 1940 to the present time. What was the total amount of capital assistance provided to this company?
The minister also stated in his address that a certain amount of that capital assistance had been purchased by the company over a period of time. Perhaps he could give us the figures as to what portion of that capital assistance had been purchased by the company, and at what discount price. Naturally they did not pay the value of the equipment


as at the time when it was put in; they must have received a certain discount.
Would he also at the same time tell us the balance of the capital assistance still outstanding, and the book value of that capital assistance at the present time? In other words' what I am trying to get at is this.
I have stated, and I think correctly, that over and above the 7-2 per cent profit admitted by the minister there is a very substantial element of subsidy to this company through this capital assistance, because the minister has already stated that the government provided certain machinery and equipment to be used in fulfilling these contracts. The company has received a profit for the fulfilling of the contracts. Therefore the use of that equipment, for which the government apparently received no other consideration, cannot be considered anything else but a subsidy over and above the 7 [DOT] 2 per cent profit. If that is not the case, the taxpayers of Canada should know what amount of subsidy goes along with that 7-2 per cent profit, so we will know actually what we are paying for this $100 million worth of guns.

Before the minister answers the question, I too was rather interested in the basis on which machinery or other equipment supplied as capital assistance was then sold to or taken over by the private industry concerned. I think the hon. member for Dauphin could have found some of his questions answered if he had read the annual report of the department. On page 27 it has this to say in this connection:
In line with the policy of encouraging private investment in defence production facilities, a number of important assets have been sold to the management companies. This is particularly true in the aircraft field where, by the end of 1955, sales of crown assets had been made to 13 companies. During 1955, negotiations were also concluded for the sale of the plant in Toronto housing the crown-owned facility for production of naval propulsion turbines.
It seems to me the picture is that if machinery and equipment are supplied to an industry then, when you make your contract for the production of goods with that industry, the consideration for the machinery is reflected in the price you are going to pay for the production of the goods. On this basis the machinery would remain as an asset in the hands of the crown. The title would remain in the crown. Then you get to the point: All right, what price do you receive when the asset is sold to the company? I think it would be very interesting to know how we fare financially at such time as the equipment is sold and turned over to the private industry concerned.
>

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I doubt if we can go back to 1940. The department we are discussing was brought into being in 1950. I think the department of munitions and supply was wound up around 1948, and where the records are now I do not know. I suppose they may be in the records building. In any event these transactions had the blessing of continuous committees of this house for several years and the records were disposed of with the approval of the government agency that decides these matters. I am willing to go back as far as the records of the department will permit, but I do not think I can go back to 1940.
Go back to 1950 at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I can do that. I shall be glad to.

I asked the minister a while ago by way of an interruption while he was speaking whether or not any other company had received the same treatment as Sorel Industries; a reward, as it were, for the period it was unoccupied and its facilities unused. Is there any other company that at the time of the Korean crisis or since has received a payment similar to the one we are discussing at the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There was no similar situation. In the case of the aircraft plant we had spent a good deal of money to keep them alive and pay the carrying costs. As I recall, the only important war plant used in the last war that was allowed to close down was Sorel Industries. We decided it was too big an obligation to take on with no certainty that the plant would ever be required again, even in the case of war.

I think I heard the minister say a few minutes ago that in 1945 the government had left some machinery in Sorel Industries. Can the minister tell us what Sorel Industries paid for the machinery left there in 1945, and also what was the original value of that machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The machinery was paid for by Sorel. We left no machinery there. Sorel bought the assets of the plant on the usual formula which is the cost of the machinery less straight line depreciation at the normal rate provided for in the income tax regulations for the period in which the machinery was used. The machinery was bought on that basis, and when the plant was closed down in 1945 we had no assets in the plant and no interest in it.

On the revenue side of the accounts there are some items which I should like to ask the minister to explain to the
25, 1956
Supply-Defence Production committee. They all relate to a transaction with Algoma Steel Corporation Limited. In the public accounts for 1952 there is reference at page DD-9 and page DD-12 to an Algoma Steel credit of $239,312.93 which is explained in these terms:
The credit in this account represents the final principal payment by the corporation in accordance with the terms of the agreement. This loan bears no interest.
Then in the 1953 public accounts at page DD-22 there is an amount of $4,401,652.26 shown under the heading, "Balances receivable under agreements of sale." In 1954 there are further entries of receipts on that account of $4 million-odd with this explanation as found at page DD-11:
This represents the balance due lor property disposed of under lease-purchase option agreement which terminates April 30, 1977, and provides for annual instalments, plus interest at 3 per cent per annum on the balance as follows . . .
Then there is a statement of the interest. Then in the public accounts for 1955 there is a final entry of receipts in this transaction. At page DD-7 under details of ordinary revenue there is an item, return on investment, Algoma Steel Corporation Limited, $123,406. That appears to be a long-range transaction, and if the minister can I wish he would give us the particulars.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It goes back to world war II. Certain facilities were put in Algoma as capital assistance facilities that Algoma did not feel justified in supplying themselves. They were supplied as capital assistance, and at the end of the war the assets were purchased by Algoma on the usual formula, cost less straight line depreciation, and the terms of the agreement obviously gave them some time to pay. Five to seven years was common, and I presume the payments referred to are payments made under these old agreements. Whether or not I can find them I do not know. The world war I stuff is not so accessible but I will see what I can find.
This is world war II.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: World war II, I should say.
Does the minister have the total cost of these facilities and the payments that were to be made by Algoma in purchasing the assets under the formula of depreciation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I cannot promise. I will get all the information I can. My hon. friend is now going back long before the department under discussion was established. The records of the old department have been

Supply-Defence Production filed away, but we will endeavour to get them and we will find out if we can.
I thank the minister, but let me point out that this is current business.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not current business for the department. When sales are made and agreements are made they become debts to the crown. The Department of Finance and the Auditor General would know about them, but the Department of Defence Production does not collect these accounts.

I am not sure how the departments divide these matters, but in the public accounts these are details under the heading, "Department of Defence Production". I assume they are matters which the Department of Defence Production keeps under its eye in order to see that the proper payments are received. If the minister could get that information, I would appreciate it. I refer to the total cost of these assets or facilities. I assume they were for the purpose of providing war materials at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I will get it if I
can. I cannot promise to do so, but I will get it if I can.

And also the prices which were paid. I have one other question along the same line. Can the minister indicate to the committee any current transactions between the department and Algoma Steel Corporation Limited.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not recall any outstanding transaction, but I will be glad to look the matter up.

Other than this one
transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was a sale of equipment installed during the second world war. I know of no similar transaction arising out of the Korean war, but I will be glad to look into the matter.

Will the minister ascertain whether the department does any current business with Algoma Steel Corporation Limited and, if so, what sort of contracts are at present being negotiated with this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As I understand it the rate the Department of National Revenue allows on machinery is 10 per cent per annum. That is under straight line depreciation. There are two methods. One is 20 per cent diminishing balance. But in transactions for the department we allow depreciation at 10 per cent per annum on a straight line basis. It is more favourable for the government.

I should like the minister to tell us what is the investment of the people of Canada and the interest they have in Sorel Industries. Is it as set out at page DD-21 of the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955? Is that amount $15,799,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, we have not any such investment.
What is the nature of these figures setting out "Investment at March 31, 1955" with respect to Sorel Industries Limited?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know what the significance is, I am sure.
That figure is to be found at page DD-21 of the public accounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think my hon. friend includes the arsenal plant at Longueuil which we own.

This is "Investment in
Plant and Equipment" and various industries across Canada are shown. Included is Sorel Industries Limited, and the figure shown is $15,799,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have the summary of capital assistance with contractors, March 31, 1956.
What is the total amount of capital assistance at the time to Sorel Industries?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The figure is $6,580,609.91.
That is since when?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is on March 31, 1956.

This report is for the year ending, March 31, 1955, and it sets out that the total amount of investment in Sorel Industries is $15,108,024. During the year it increased by $931,000, and there were transfers of capital assets and the investment in this country is $15,799,000. I just wondered whether or not that referred to the answer to the question that was asked a while ago by the hon. member for Dauphin, and represented the amount the government of Canada has advanced to this company through the years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, that would not be the answer. He was asking what the investment in the company was from 1940. As I say, the investment up to 1945 was liquidated by a payment from the company to the government which transferred all the property to them. I am not just clear. Sorel Industries expanded their capacity by taking over a plant that the government owns in Longueuil, outside of Montreal. The only thing I can think of is that there must have been a combination of these two plants. But of course Longueuil is owned by the government and always was owned by the government, and all the equipment in it is owned by the government. I will send this sheet across to my hon. friend.
If the minister would just turn to the public accounts and give me an explanation of what this $15 million figure is, I should be obliged. It is to be found at page DD-25.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry, but I have not a copy of the public accounts.
I will send this copy over to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Longueuil plant under this account is charged to Sorel. That is, it is put in the keeping of Sorel; it is turned over to Sorel for operation. Nevertheless the Longueuil plant and everything in it is owned by the government and will continue to be owned by the government.
The minister's figures a moment ago were some $6 million as the amount as of March 31, 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is right.
67509-409i
Supply-Defence Production
How does he account for the difference? What has happened during the last year whereby the indebtedness of Sorel has been reduced from $15 million to $6 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was never an indebtedness. This is simply a list of crown assets charged to the various companies.
That would be indebtedness, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is not a debt. It just shows that certain government capital assets are in their keeping. It is not a debt until the government sells the assets to them. If the government owns it, it can take it out. It is not a debt. That Longueuil plant in the figure quoted from public accounts was obviously charged to Sorel Industries Limited.
How much was the value of the Longueuil plant charged to Sorel Industries?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It must have been the difference; $9 million, probably.
Has the minister the figures there among his papers? That seems to be a lot of millions.
He is just guessing at $9 million.
That is so.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Longueuil plant was built for the government. It was operated by the government during the second world war, and in fact after the second world war. When it was found that additional space was needed for heavy guns, operations there were transferred to the Quebec arsenals plant and this plant was turned over to Sorel Industries. I am sure that at that time the plant and the equipment in the plant were listed under Sorel industries, although it was government property.

If the minister would just find out from his officials why there Js this difference between $15 million and $6 million in a year? What was the amount for the Longueuil plant? The minister said approximately $9 million. I would ask him if he would get the exact figures in that connection, because he apparently has them before him?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, I have not. We have the Sorel figure, but not the Longueuil plant. The Longueuil plant was built about 1940 or 1941 and it has always been owned by the government.

Supply-Defence Production

It still does not explain the $15 million for March 31, 1955, and how that $15 million item was made up? Did it include the Longueuil plant, and if so what portion of the $15 million represented the Longueuil plant? It is quite a large item, and one would expect some kind of a breakdown of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I gave the amount that was listed for the Sorel plant. We have it here. The balance must have been the Longueuil plant, but we will be glad to look up the original figure and tell you how it came about.
Of course $9 million is quite a lot, I would think.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I know, but the Longueuil plant does not enter into these estimates. It has not been operated by the department.
When was the Longueuil plant taken over by Sorel Industries?
What does this company, Sorel Industries, pay for the equipment and for the Longueuil plant? Has the minister got that? It must surely pay something for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Longueuil plant was used for government work and we were not charged anything for it. I do not know whether they paid anything. I would be glad to look that up. My hon. friend wants to go back over about $17 billion worth of contracts and expects me to have the information-
No, this is March 31. 1955.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -expects me to remember the details of every one of the contracts that made up the $17 billion. I cannot do it, I will tell you frankly. If you will give me the definite information you want I will endeavour to get it. I am sure I can get most of it. If you want to go back into the dim past, to 1940 or 1941, I am not sure I can get it because I imagine those records are in central storage.
I know my hon. friend once said, "What is a million?"

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a fiction that has been plastered all across the country by my hon. friend.
You originated it.
No, as a matter of fact I have kept it out of sight at all times. I would not refer to it at all, but I am saying it was said.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Even Maclean's magazine took the trouble to go back to try to get the origin of it. Now it has been exposed to the public, but my hon. friend keeps on saying, "What's a million?"
We all heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It was never said.
We heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend now has made a statement, and I can pin him down on this statement. You find the exact page of Hansard where I said that and produce it, and I will resign my seat and go to the country.
Has there been an expurgation job done on Hansard?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend makes these statements, and this is only typical of the statements he makes every day. This happens to be one on which I can pin him down, and perhaps he will apologize.
We all heard it.
Who has the floor now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend appreciates a fabrication.

I would appreciate your
making a correct statement. We heard you say, "What's a million dollars?"
I heard it myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Surely these
people had better put up now. You are very intelligent people with lots of spare time. While you are sitting around here trying to keep the government here by stringing out this session, surely you have time to go through Hansard and find this reference. We do not mind sitting here, you know. We realize that only five or six members run the house and the rest are up in their offices. Surely they could take half an hour and find that quotation?

I am not concerned about that million which did not amount to anything, but I am concerned about this $15 million that appears in the public accounts as the investment of the people of Canada in Sorel Industries, and charged to Sorel Industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It does not say so.

It would not appear there if the dominion government had not some interest. I have asked the minister a very simple question; how much was charged for this Longueuil plant? What was the value of the Longueuil plant? The minister says, "I have not got figures like that."

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend is on item No. 1, when general speeches are made. Am I supposed to have all the figures he can think of asking me to produce? I will get those figures and I will produce them, but I cannot do it now. I do not remember them, and I have not the information before me. I can give him the amount charged to the plant at Sorel, but I cannot give him a breakdown of the amount charged to Sorel Industries.

I want to ask a question and I am sure the minister can answer it, because he does not have to dig through figures to do so. It is a matter of policy. I refer to the same matter now under discussion, this investment of $15 million of public funds in Sorel Industries, or in any private company. What is the policy of the government? What consideration does the government receive on behalf of the public treasury in return for putting that investment in the hands of a private company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Lower profit is allowed. The profit margin is reduced in proportion to the amount of government-owned machinery that is used. The end product costs less because no depreciation for the equipment is charged. For instance, if a plant buys its equipment and additional profit is allowed the plant because it owns its own equipment. These adjustments are made as a matter of routine. We might pay a light industry 4 per cent for operation with government equipment, and if it buys equipment we might pay 5 per cent or 5 * 5 per cent.

That is very interesting and very important, because I think it is important that the public should know on what basis these industries are paid for the contract they undertake for producing these materials.
Let me ask this question. The minister says a consideration is that the profit is not as great where there is an investment by the public in the form of equipment. At what point is that decision arrived at? For example, let us say the government lets a contract in 1955 for a certain quantity of guns. In letting that contract to a private firm, is it a firm contract on which a margin of profit is provided, or is there a total price provided, or is that an open contract to be adjusted at the time of completion? What type of contract is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It depends on the nature of the contract. If it is let by competitive tender of course it is a firm price. If it is for a product that must be built in a particular plant, there are many ways of getting it done and often the profit is to be
Supply-Defence Production adjusted. For instance, in aircraft production we have a starting rate and it is adjusted. As the learning curve proceeds and efficiency goes up the rate of profit is adjusted. It is a very complex business. I do not think I can explain it on the floor of the house. Perhaps I do not know it well enough myself to explain it, but we have a pattern in these things. If my hon. friend would like to have a committee next year I am sure my officers would be very glad to go there and they would be able to go into this thing. With the right kind of talent there and sitting as long as you like we could let the committee decide whether it is right or wrong, and not come back to the house and ask me to decide.

If I may pursue one more question, I should like to point out to the minister that these are not the kind of questions on which we can obtain information in a committee, particularly in the public accounts committee, because they involve government policy. It is well known that officials of a particular department will not answer questions involving government policy, and I think quite rightly so. That is the responsibility of the minister concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend is not asking me policy questions; he is asking me questions for information, questions of fact. I would be glad to answer policy questions, but that is not what he is asking.

I shall change the question slightly. Will the minister place before this committee the policy that is followed with respect to government contracts in the industries in which the government has an investment in the form of equipment such as, for example, Sorel Industries? I would suggest to him that perhaps the best way it could be done-he tells us it is a complex business, and no doubt it is, but that is all the more reason why the public should know all about it- would be to table one or two typical contracts so that all the terms of the contract would then be known. They could be used as an example. He could choose the contracts that would be the most typical, and then the public would have an opportunity to know exactly on what basis we are paying these companies.
At the present time I am firmly convinced that the margin of profit admitted or stated is not the true margin of profit, because there is an element of subsidy on account of the fact that there is this equipment supplied and paid for by the public treasury for which the government or the treasury receives no consideration. That must be added to the overall profit because there seems to be no other place to put it. If an example of a contract

Supply-Defence Production could be tabled so we could see ourselves just where that consideration comes, just where those adjustments are made that the minister mentioned, then I for one would be satisfied, and that is definitely a matter of government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure there are hundreds of contracts filed with the Clerk of this house. Every contract is tabled in this house. I do not know what more I can table than is tabled.
Did I understand the minister to say that every contract has been tabled in this house?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; a number have been tabled. For instance, at every meeting of the defence expenditures committee a number of contracts have been tabled. If my hnn. friend will tell me that he wants a particular contract tabled I will be glad to table it. A report of the department indicates how many separate contracts were made during the year, and I know it runs into hundreds of thousands. Just to pick out one is difficult. Why does my hon. friend not pick out one?

I will be glad to do that. If the minister would table the contract with respect to the guns manufactured by Sorel Industries that has been mentioned here this afternoon, that one would be quite satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told that all these contracts were tabled in the public accounts committee. Is my hon. friend a member of that committee?
I never saw them tabled.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told they were tabled; I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I would like to continue to discuss the point raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert, the hon. member for Eglin-ton and the hon. member for Calgary North. All three hon. gentlemen say they remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce saying, "What's a million?" We all know, of course, how inaccurate is the memory of the hon. member for Eglinton. The Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that the Tories, since they have mentioned it so often, should go and get Hansard and show that he said, "What's a million?"
None of them moved, so I went out to the library and very quickly got Hansard for the second session of 1945, shortly after the hon. member for Eglinton entered the house. Here is the famous remark which the hon. member for Eglinton was so sure the minister made and so arrogantly said he remembered distinctly, as did the hon. member for Calgary

North. The discussion was on the estimates of the then minister of munitions and supply. At page 2251 of Hansard the minister had this to say:
I call the attention of my hon. friend-
His hon. friend is the financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Greenwood. I notice that the hon. member for Eglinton is aspiring to that job in the absence of the hon. member for Greenwood.
No, he is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
You are not worthy to aspire to fill his shoes. I continue:
I call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that we are dealing with an over-all bill for some $1,365 million. This is only a break-down for purposes of discussion, and this amount is not being appropriated by itself: a bill in which this is included is being prepared. I dare say my hon. friend could cut a million dollars from this amount:	but a million dollars from the war
appropriation bill would not be a very important matter.

I suppose that is true.
On an estimate of $1,365 million, $1 million is about one-tenth of one per cent, or a little less. This is the statement which the hon. member for Eglinton has just said he distinctly recalls being, "What's a million?"

The arrogant Minister of Fisheries has just made one of his statements that has a very fishy flavour to it. Mr. Chairman, what particular passage the Minister of Fisheries has dug out in compliance with whatever request he received from the Minister of Defence Production will have to be his responsibility; but whether that is a passage about the same time or not, the fact is that members of this house did hear the statement, and it is a curious thing-*

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You produce it.
-that here we are at July 25, 1956-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a falsehood.

This statement, attributed to the Minister of Defence Production, "What's a million dollars?" has been referred to in this house and elsewhere, I suppose, hundreds and hundreds if not thousands of times; it has been quoted many times in the hearing of the minister and this is the first time he has been prompted to suggest that he never made the statement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: It has been denied before.
It is a curious delay, Mr. Chairman, a long delay.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend makes so many speeches and delivers so many falsehoods.

There he is on his feet. The rules do not mean a thing. He is up on his feet cutting into the middle of other people's speeches. He is not satisfied to let anybody else make a speech. The rules are only for other people; they are not for him. He has his cackling chorus taking up the story. There they go; there they are.
Now, Mr. Chairman, members of this house have made their comments. The Minister of Fisheries has brought up a passage and he is asking the house to say that is the only statement the minister has ever said that comes close to the one attributed to him. Well, statements by members have been made here this afternoon, and I do not know that anybody is going to change his statement. I certainly do not intend to, Mr. Chairman. I comment again; it was a curious demonstration; it is an amazing demonstration. After this famous statement has been carried right across this country; it has been discussed, I suppose, or referred to on every election platform or on the hustings for the last decade, and it has been referred to in this house on more than one occasion. Yet the minister, in this year of grace 1956, has suddenly discovered that somebody has made the statement that he made the statement, and he says now he did not make the statement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Which is true.
There may be a lot of credulous people in this house, Mr. Chairman, but I think this strains credulity beyond all possible recognition.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I can perhaps answer this, too, because the hon. member for Eglinton has once again displayed his amazing ignorance about other people's speeches. He knows his own speeches very well because he keeps requoting them to us.
You have never heard me quote from one of my own speeches.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The first time this was mentioned was in the 1949 budget speech of the financial critic of the Tory party who was then the member for Muskoka, I think it was, and who is now the hon. member for Greenwood. In the course of his speech he claimed the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said, "What's a million?" That was my first year as parliamentary assistant. I looked up the remark then and answered him immediately. That was the reason I could find this so quickly, not because I remembered my own speech. I went to the library and found my speech and came back with the answer in Hansard of 1945. At that time I put on the record not only what the Minister of Trade
Supply-Defence Production and Commerce had said in 1945 but what happened, and the Tory party has been lying about it from that day on.

Mr. Chairman, the fishy remark we have just heard does not affect in the least the facts as stated here this afternoon, and it is not going to deter anyone who heard the remark that has been referred to from referring to it whenever it pleases him to do so.
Whether it is right or wrong.
The remark has been referred to on many occasions in this house and the minister has not denied it in 11 years. I fail to understand, Mr. Chairman, what has given rise-
Order.
-to this very interesting situation where suddenly out of the blue, on July 25-
The year is 1956.
-1956, apparently someone around the minister suddenly becomes conscious of the fact-

Perhaps they read
Maclean's magazine.

Yes. This remark has been referred to for 11 years, but it is only today that the minister pretends he has suddenly become aware of it. How extraordinary! It is just too much for human credulity, even the Liberal variety.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: One last suggestion, Mr. Chairman. I would suggest that this little pocket Mussolini put up or shut up. Let him now find the remark in Hansard; let him quote the minister using the words, "What's a million dollars?"
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I do recall that in the last parliament the Speaker of that house, when I chose to draw certain comparisons between the attitude of one Mussolini and the Minister of Defence Production, thought it was an unparliamentary sort of remark and-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member only referred to you as a pocket Mussolini, though.
Pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He only referred to you as a pocket Mussolini; that is different.

Well, I shall refer to the minister as a great big overgrown, overstuffed Mussolini.

Supply-Defence Production
He is certainly not overgrown.
Mr. Chairman, I have said what I have said, and I stand by what I have said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Which is nothing.
I am not the least bit impressed by these remarks of the sullen Minister of Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Put up or shut up.
We have had some examples that hon. members have not forgotten when surgical operations were performed on Hansard by the ministers this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Back in 1945?

If those words I have referred to are not readily available in Hansard, then I can only infer that somebody has gone back and performed a surgical operation on Hansard similar to the one that was performed-
Name it.
-this session by the Minister f Agriculture.
How low can you get?
You ought to know.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River. Order. I think I should apologize to both hon. gentlemen. The hon. member for The Battlefords rose a moment ago and I incorrectly identified him as the hon. member for Bow River. The hon. member for Bow River also has a question and perhaps he would permit the hon. member for The Battlefords to speak first.
Mr. Chairman, I was just going to ask you if you could not get the house back to business.

Mr. Chairman, my question will not be much longer than that of the hon. member for The Battlefords. I would like to ask the minister a question concerning the payment that was given to Sorel Industries in view of their being idle for the five year period. I understood the minister to say that after 1945, when the government informed Sorel they would not be getting any more orders and therefore they should turn their plant over to peacetime production, they had received offers to dispose of their machinery and came to the minister to get his opinion regarding it. If


I understood the minister correctly he said he advised them not to do that.
If that is so, then I would think the minister would have had to indicate to them the reason for saying that. Probably the reason would be, "Well, you should not dispose of the machinery because later on we may want"-and I use the word "may" advisedly-"to place an order for guns or something of that sort, and then you would have the plant ready".
If that is a proper inference and if that were said to the company, then I think in 1950 when the government came to Sorel and said, "Now here is an order we want you to fill" probably the Sorel company would be in a position-and rightly so-to say to the government, "You advised us not to dispose of our machinery but to hold it until such time as you placed an order with us.
