Therefore by right you should pay at least something for maintaining our plant and machinery up to this time". Is that the situation or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, no, I think that is putting it too strongly, really. They came to me and wanted to know what the view of the government would be about a prospective sale they had to another government. I said this government would not like it. I did not intend to intimate that if they did not make the sale we would probably use the machinery. I did not suggest that for a moment. Nevertheless, while we were unwilling to take any risk on having the machinery maintained in 1945, when we realized in 1949 that we were going to need the plant we took a different view of the situation. We felt something should be done to put the plant on something resembling a basis of equality with other plants and that we should bear a portion of the cost of maintaining the plant during the period it was closed down. That decision was made in 1949, but it was not determined by anything said in the past; at least I did not so consider it.

I have another question to ask the minister, and it does not relate to Sorel Industries. I notice in the estimates that the amount to be paid is $22,002,628. I wonder if the minister could tell us the share each of the provinces receives out of this estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am afraid we cannot make a provincial breakdown. The difficulty is that the main contract is placed in one province but subcontracts may go to other provinces. Raw materials, for instance, may come from other provinces. We find we cannot make a breakdown) concerning

defence purchasing that means very much as far as a division among the provinces is concerned.

I do not expect the minister could go into a detailed division, because I understand raw materials may come from one place and other materials from another; but I should not think it would be very difficult for the minister to say what portion of the contracts that are let are allocated to the various provinces. How much was given to Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and so on? I would think that information would be very easy to obtain.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We do not keep records in that way for the reason given. For instance, a great many companies maintain head offices in Ottawa and their contracts are signed here. So far as we know they are Ottawa firms, but if we trace it back we find they are not Ottawa firms; they may be Halifax firms, for all we know. The records of the department just do not allow an accurate breakdown of work as between the provinces.

Perhaps I could put it this way. It is not my purpose to embarrass the minister, but I should like to know what share of this $20 million-odd is received by industries in Alberta. I do not think we get any of it. It seems to me that this is an opportunity to encourage industrial development in all the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My hon. friend realizes that this $22 million is really an administration vote. It does not buy anything. There is $6 million for departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production. That is practically all spent in Ottawa; a little perhaps elsewhere. There is an amount of $500,000 for care, maintenance and custody of stand-by defence plants, buildings, machine tools and production tooling. That depends on where the closed-down production plant is; it could be traced, perhaps. There is $7,500,000 for capital assistance. That varies from year to year. The bulk of it is in connection with the CF-105 program and it is mostly spent in the province of Ontario; I should think it is practically all spent there. The payment of grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on crown-owned defence plants is spread around the provinces, and that would apply wherever there are government-owned defence plants.
Under crown companies there is Defence Construction Limited. Some of that has probably been spent in Alberta. That is the work
Supply-Defence Production of supervising defence contracts that occur during the year. Then there is Canadian Arsenals Limited. I do not think there is any arsenal plant in the west now. There used to be one at Calgary but there is none there now. I should not think that any of that is spent in Alberta. I should think my hon. friend is correct in saying that practically none of this vote is spent in Alberta.

On the question raised by the hon. member for Bow River, I referred during another debate to sessional paper 237A, in which it was estimated that British Columbia was going to get $221,000 in defence production. I am wondering how they arrived at that particular figure in view of the answer that was given to the hon. member for Bow River. Referring to that specific figure at this time, it strikes me as rather difficult to understand. Here is a province, as I said in another debate, with one-tenth of Canada's population, getting an appropriation of approximately $221,000, which must have been arrived at by this department or it would not have appeared on the sessional paper, out of a total of some $22 million. That would be about 1 per cent of the total.
My question is this. I am wondering what consideration, if any, is given the placement of these contracts on a geographical basis. I am thinking more particularly, of course, not just of the net returns that are received by a province but of the matter of defence itself, and the fact that it would help labour in some of the more distant areas. I am not thinking specifically so much of the case of British Columbia; it could apply to any one of the provinces.
It would seem to me, whilst I can understand the minister's explanation up to a point, that here we have an instance of a contract possibly being let in Ottawa and then sublet in British Columbia. Indirectly they are getting some of it, and if the main office for that particular company happens to be in Ottawa, then British Columbia would be directly benefiting from it. But you have instances such as took place last year, where a firm in Quebec-I forget the name-was given a contract to make pallets. I understand they made some 750,000 in Quebec and sent them around through the Panama canal or some other way to British Columbia to be used in North Vancouver. It seems to me that there was no subletting of a contract there. Where we have the lumber and everything else required, I was wondering why these things are not let on a geographical basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
When my hon. friend suggests that British Columbia does not get its share of defence contracts, I

Supply-Defence Production think he is hardly giving his province proper credit. For instance, I think British Columbia has a good share of all the naval shipbuilding in Canada, and shipbuilding is a very big part of defence. It has a very good share of defence airports. Of all the installations for defence throughout Canada, I think British Columbia has had its full share.
As far as the much discussed pallets are concerned, the fact of the matter is that we called for tenders for pallets delivered at Vancouver. We found that a firm in Quebec could make the pallets in Quebec, pay the freight to Vancouver and beat the price of pallets made in Vancouver. We did not believe it when we got the answer, but we found that it happened again, and so we placed the order accordingly. We are given a delivery point, and the terms of purchases are freight paid to delivery point, we think there is no reason to give the local manufacturer the job of making the pallets at an increased cost in spite of the advantage he gets from being on the spot rather than being 3,000 miles away.

I am very pleased with the answer the minister has given in respect to the pallets. It certainly explains a point that possibly contractors in British Columbia should keep in mind when they are bidding for some of these contracts.
The question I have in mind now is, how did this figure of $221,000 appear in sessional paper 237A if, as the minister says, British Columbia is getting its share of the contract? Certainly there is $22 million in contracts here. I should think that the $221,000 should include all the enterprises of which the minister spoke a moment ago. I can think of no way in which that figure would get on to the sessional paper unless it came from his department. Just a few moments ago, however, he told the hon. member for Bow River, as I understand it, that there was no way of breaking it down.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The hon. member is perhaps referring to the items that I read from the estimate book. These are not expenditures for contracts; they are services. For instance, the first item is for salaries paid to people who work for the department. I suppose we have perhaps a dozen or 15 people stationed in British Columbia who draw their salaries there. The next item is care, maintenance and custody of stand-by defence plants. I do not think we have in British Columbia any such defence plants. The next item is capital assistance, but there probably does not happen to be any capital assistance provided for British Columbia for this year. The next item is grants to municipalities. They would be comparatively small.


I am not sure whether we have any crown-owned plants there. The next item refers to Canadian Arsenals; and the arsenals are all in the east. Then there is Defence Construction Limited. There would be a share of that spent in British Columbia. Perhaps part of the amount mentioned is for salaries for inspection of defence projects there. Those are all the items covered by the $22 million. I am not surprised that the part of this particular $22 million spent in British Columbia is as stated in the return. The greater part of it is spent in Ottawa, right in this city.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No; January, 1954, was the peak of the revolving fund. At that time there was $111 million out; as of March 31, 1955, $70 million, and March 31, 1956, $59 million. If the present activity is maintained or the downward tendency continues, it appears possible to operate within the statutory maximum of $100 million, and on that basis the supplemental $50 million

would seem superfluous. Incidentally, we do not keep that money in the bank in a special account. We have the right to draw down up to these limits, but, as I say, as things appear now we could drop $50 million from that authorization.

Well, as I understand the effect of the fund, the $100 million and the amount in item 825 of the supplementary estimates of 1951-52, by reason of the provisions of the act are available for the continued operation of the revolving fund. In other words, it is not like a normal annual vote. The act itself makes provision for the addition to the revolving fund, and unless there is some amending bill brought in the $50 million continues to be available as part of the revolving fund.
It is quite clear from what the minister has said, I think, that there has been no drawing on that additional $50 million for a couple of years now, and that the commitments on the revolving fund are likely to be reduced from this point on. Therefore I raise directly the question as to whether the time has not come for the return of that $50 million. In other words, surely the $100 million in the original act would be adequate, and parliament would be justified now in withdrawing the additional $50 million as being no longer necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not mind bringing in a bill at the next session to reduce the amount available to the revolving fund. I realize that if the money is not used it remains there unused; but my concern is to maintain the principle of parliamentary control. In regard to expenditures out of revolving funds there is, I think, a particular reason, because revolving funds sometimes are hard to reconcile with the principle of parliamentary control. Now, the book of estimates would appear to indicate that the department on this large first item of administration is budgeting for a reduction from $6,391,430 last year to $6,145,727 this year. In other words the book of estimates shows a decrease of $245,703. But it is always well to look beyond those figures to get the figures of actual expenditures, and here we find that the amount actually.spent by the department, the amount that was adequate to cover all the needs of this department under the administration item, was $5,831,835, which indicates that the department this year is not budgeting for a decrease as compared with last year's actual requirements, Mr. Chairman, but that the department is actually budgeting for an increase of $314,000; for the difference between this year's estimates of $6,145,727 and last year's actual expenditure of $5,831,835, according to my arithmetic, indicates the department is asking approval this year of a sum $314,000 larger than was spent last year. Therefore I ask the minister what

Supply-Defence Production accounts for the increase? Is there anything more that enters into the increase than increases in salary rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is an increase of about 5 per cent. I do not think you would need to go beyond the increase in salary rates to make up the difference of 5 per cent.

The number on the staff of the department is almost the same as the year before, according to the book of estimates. If the minister says this is simply an increase in salary rates that is his explanation, but I do draw attention to the fact that on this item the department is budgeting not for a decrease, as the book of estimates would indicate, but for an actual increase over last year's expenditure.
The next question, Mr. Chairman, was in regard to the basis of purchase. I drew attention to the sentence on page 24 of the annual report of the department, which reads:
With the increase in Canada's industrial defence potential it has been possible to purchase more goods in Canada, to increase the number of cases in which contracts are placed on the basis of competitive tender, and to move from cost plus to target price or negotiated firm price contracts in those fields in which Canadian firms have gained more operating experience.
Looking at that statement I asked, as indicated at page 5524 of Hansard, for detailed information on the number and value and proportion of the total of contracts placed on competitive tender and the numbers and amounts and percentages of those placed on a cost plus basis, or a target price basis, or negotiated firm price basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1956, over 116,000 orders were placed as a result of competitive tenders. In terms of value these contracts represented about 60 per cent of all contracts placed by the department during that period, a very appreciable improvement over the previous year when some 30 per cent by value were based on competitive tender.
The analysis of non-competitive or negotiated contracts for the last fiscal year shows that most of these contracts in terms of value were placed by the head office of the department. Contracts amounting to $242 million were in this category, while the balance of non-competitive contracts amounting to $11 million were placed by the district offices of the department.
Of the $242 million, $41 million were on the basis of firm price, $55 million were on the basis of cost plus, $14 million were ceiling contracts and $2 million were target price.
Would you give the third figure again, please?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Fourteen million dollars were on ceiling contracts. The balance of $130 million were placed on a price to be negotiated basis and have not been finalized.
Of the $11 million placed by district offices no breakdown is available, but most of these contracts would be under $10,000 and would be for items for which there is only one source of supply; for instance, spare parts for the repair or maintenance of items used by the services.
I would like to point out that because a contract is negotiated it does not follow that the terms are less favourable to the government. Rates of profit are maintained at fair and reasonable levels, and in many cases the department is receiving discounts that are equal to or more than those allowed by the contractor to his most favoured customer. Moreover, in most non-competitive orders an audit is performed and certain qualifications are imposed by the department on the determination of the costs upon which the agreed rate of profit is to be applied. Does that answer the question?

Yes. I thank the minister for that information. There is one thing I did not get clear as the minister was reading over the figures. I believe the minister said that 116,000 orders were placed as competitive orders which constituted 60 per cent of all contracts. Was that in number or amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: By value.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that all hon. members would be glad to see an increase in the proportion of total business the department is doing which is now being done by competitive tender. May I ask the minister if the outlook is such that he considers this desirable trend may be expected to continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, it is doubtful. For instance, all the equipment for the mid-Canada line is very secret and the location of the sites is secret. It is impossible to do other than negotiate a contract. The CF-105 is similar, and we are breaking new ground there with a new aircraft. It is quite impossible, of course, to get anything like a target. All you can do there is proceed on the basis of cost plus until you get to the production stage; then after that there is a target arranged for a certain number of planes and a lower target is arranged for subsequent ones as the curve goes down. For defence procurement there is a limit to the amount of equipment that may be purchased by competitive tender. It means there must be at least two sources of the material before you can get competitive tenders.
Are we to infer that the minister thinks we now have hit the maximum in the proportion of contracts placed by competitive tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, but we have hit a level where I would say it would be a toss up whether the percentage for next year would be greater or less. It depends entirely on the predominance of the work and the nature of it.

The next question relates to the Defence Production Act. As indicated at page 5523 of Hansard, I asked the minister how many orders have been made under that act, and I asked for their listing or classification under the various sections of the act. In other words, as I said at that time, what orders have been issued under each of the sections of the act conferring powers upon the government or the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No orders are now in effect.
Excuse me, but the period I have in mind would be, let us say, from the beginning of 1955. If the minister has more figures we had probably better hear them first.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
All the orders were revoked before 1955. There are no orders now in effect. The only orders issued under those sections of the Defence Production Act conferring powers on the Canadian government or the Minister of Defence Production are those covering the designation and control of essential materials. These consist of orders in council under section 30 of the act and orders of the minister under section 31 of the act. Other sections of the act referred to above are 21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 33. No orders were issued under any of these sections.
I can give my hon. friend a list of the orders that have been issued since April, 1951, to
25,	1956
Supply-Defence Production May 31, 1954. The last one was issued on May 31, 1954.
Perhaps it might be convenient, Mr. Chairman, and would save time, if the list were put on Hansard without taking the time to read it, if that is the wish of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They have all been revoked and I doubt if it is worth cluttering up Hansard with that information. There is a long list here, but they are all orders that expired not later than 1954.
I would be satisfied if the minister could supply a copy to those hon. members who are interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will be glad to do so. I will give my hon. friend this copy if he wants it.

Mr. Chairman, it is six o'clock and I would just make this one comment on the minister's last answer. It has not been found necessary by the government or the minister to issue a single order under this act since the debate a year ago on the continuation of the minister's powers under this act, and I think that is an eloquent tribute to the position taken by the opposition at that time on this matter.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No. It is six o'clock.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
